title: [misc] Orphan cleanup removes the active entity but never completes its CompletableFuture -> caller hangs forever
description:
/Users/hal.hildebrand/git/Luciferase/simulation/src/main/java/com/hellblazer/luciferase/simulation/distributed/migration/CrossProcessMigration.java:431-450
Severity: High | Category: concurrency

title: [simulation] Locale-dependent String.format(%f) emits malformed JSON for centroids/densityRatio in non-US locales
description:

moveEventToJson (lines 162-171) and densityStateChangeEventToJson (lines 173-180) build JSON via String.format(...) without a Locale argument, using %f for centroid coordinates and densityRatio. String.format uses the default locale; in locales that use comma as the decimal separator (e.g. de_DE, fr_FR) %f produces e.g. 1,5 instead of 1.5, yielding invalid JSON like {"x":1,500000,...}. title: [misc] Migration failure metric double-counted (executeMigration records failure, caller records it again)
description:
/Users/hal.hildebrand/git/Luciferase/simulation/src/main/java/com/hellblazer/luciferase/simulation/bubble/TetrahedralMigration.java:228, 262, 141
Severity: High | Category: CORRECTNESS

executeMigration() calls metrics.recordFailedMigration() internally on the null-bubble path (line 228) and on the rollback path (line 262) before returning false. The caller checkMigrations() then ALSO calls metrics.recordFailedMigration() because executeMigration returned false (line 141). So failureCount is incremented twice for every src/dst-null and rollback-failure migration. getFailureCount() (TetrahedralMigrationMetrics.getFailureCount) therefore over-reports failures, corrupting any test or operator dashboard keyed on it and masking the true failure rate.

Fix: Pick one owner of the failure metric. Remove the recordFailedMigration() calls inside executeMigration (lines 228, 262, 272) and let checkMigrations own all failure recording via its return-value branch; or vice versa. Add a unit test asserting failureCount == exact expected N (not >0) after a forced null-route and a forced rollback.

Because both return false, the caller increments again at line 141, so failureCount is incremented twice per src/dst-null and per rollback-failure migration. This over-reports failures and corrupts getFailureCount-keyed dashboards/tests. Severity High is appropriate: it is a metric-correctness defect (not silent data loss / crash), affects observability and any failure-rate-keyed assertions, and the double-count is deterministic on those code paths. Note: the routing-failed path (line 145) and the entity-not-found path (line 240-241) are correctly single-counted, but the two specifically cited paths (228 and 262) are genuinely double-counted as described.

title: [render] readIntArray treats a single FileChannel.read as complete — spurious IOException on valid large files
description:
render/src/main/java/com/hellblazer/luciferase/sparse/io/SparseVoxelIOUtils.java:97-101
Severity: High | Category: correctness / partial-read

readIntArray allocates count*4 bytes, does ONE channel.read(buffer), and throws IOException if bytesRead != count*4. FileChannel.read is permitted to return fewer bytes than the buffer's remaining capacity even when more data is available (large reads, blocking channels, sockets-as-channels). For large voxel int arrays this will throw 'Expected N bytes, read M' on perfectly valid data, corrupting load of any sufficiently large sparse-voxel file. Separately, count*4 is an int multiply: count > ~536M overflows to negative/wrong, making the length check and allocation wrong (DoS / silent truncation).

Fix: Loop until the buffer is full (while (buffer.hasRemaining()) { int n = channel.read(buffer); if (n < 0) throw EOF; }) instead of a single read. Compute the byte count as a long (long bytes = (long) count * 4) for the comparison and guard against overflow before allocate.

Verify evidence: Confirmed by reading render/src/main/java/com/hellblazer/luciferase/sparse/io/SparseVoxelIOUtils.java lines 97-101. The code is verbatim: `var buffer = ByteBuffer.allocate(count * 4).order(BYTE_ORDER); int bytesRead = channel.read(buffer); if (bytesRead != count * 4) { throw new IOException("Expected " + (count * 4) + " bytes, read " + bytesRead); }`. Both flaws are genuine. (1) Partial-read: FileChannel.read(ByteBuffer) is contractually permitted to return fewer bytes than the buffer's remaining capacity; the correct idiom loops until the buffer is full or EOF (-1). This single-read check throws a spurious IOException on valid data, corrupting load of any sufficiently large sparse-voxel int array. (2) Integer overflow: count is int and `count * 4` is evaluated in int arithmetic, so count > ~536M overflows to a negative/wrong value, breaking both ByteBuffer.allocate(count*4) and the length comparison (DoS / silent truncation). The symmetric writeIntArray (line 76/81) shares the int*4 overflow and trusts a single channel.write. Severity High is appropriate — this is a real correctness/data-integrity defect on the file-load path; note the partial-read manifestation is latent for mode

title: [misc] Deserialization filter restricts classes but sets no resource limits (maxbytes/maxarray/maxdepth/maxrefs) -> OOM DoS amplification
description:
/Users/hal.hildebrand/git/Luciferase/simulation/src/main/java/com/hellblazer/luciferase/simulation/von/transport/VonTransportFilter.java:47-59
Severity: High | Category: security

VonTransportFilter.PATTERN is a pure class allow-list ending in '!*'. It allows java.util.ArrayList and java.lang.* (String). ObjectInputFilter resource-limit directives (maxbytes=, maxarray=, maxdepth=, maxrefs=) are entirely absent, and SocketServer.handleClient (SocketServer.java:143-146) reads readObject() off an untrusted network socket with no SO_TIMEOUT and no length prefix. A malicious or buggy peer can send a single serialized TransportVonMessage carrying a gigantic ArrayList of Strings (all allow-listed types) or a deeply nested/back-referenced graph and exhaust heap before the (TransportVonMessage) cast. This is the Java-serialization analogue of a missing gRPC maxInboundMessageSize: the class allow-list closes the RCE gadget vector (RDR-004) but leaves the resource-exhaustion vector wide open. Loopback-only binding (SocketServer.java:102) is the only mitigation, and it is explicitly slated to be lifted (Inc 7+).

Fix: Append resource caps to PATTERN, e.g. 'maxbytes=<N>;maxarray=<N>;maxdepth=<N>;maxrefs=<N>;' (sized to the largest legitimate GhostSync/JoinResponse payload), and set clientSocket.setSoTimeout(...) in SocketServer.handleClient so a slow-loris / stalled read cannot pin a thread+socket forever.

VonTransportFilter.PATTERN (lines 47-59) is a pure class allow-list terminated by "!*" with NO resource-limit directives: it allows "java.util.ArrayList;" (line 53) and "java.lang.*;" (line 56, admits String) but contains no maxbytes=, maxarray=, maxdepth=, or maxrefs= clauses. ObjectInputFilter.Config.createFilter(PATTERN) (line 68) therefore enforces class restrictions only, applying zero resource limits. SocketServer.handleClient (lines 142-149) reads (TransportVonMessage) stream.readObject() in a loop off an untrusted client socket; the filter is installed (line 144) but the resource-exhaustion vector remains open. No SO_TIMEOUT is set and there is no length prefix. A peer can send a single serialized graph using only allow-listed types (e.g. a gigantic ArrayList of Strings, or a deeply nested / back-referenced graph) and exhaust heap during deserialization before the cast — the Java-serialization analogue of a missing gRPC maxInboundMessageSize. The class allow-list does close the RCE gadget vector (RDR-004), but leaves resource-exhaustion DoS undefended. The loopback-only binding (lines 102-106) is the sole present-day mitigation and the i
notes: ENRICHED 2026-06-04 | still-valid: yes | anchors: VonTransportFilter.java:47-59 PATTERN is pure class allow-list ending in '!*' (ArrayList :53, java.lang.* :56); NO maxbytes/maxarray/maxdepth/maxrefs anywhere. SocketServer.java:116 serverSocket.accept(), :146 (TransportVonMessage) stream.readObject() on untrusted socket; NO setSoTimeout call anywhere in SocketServer; loopback-only gate at :97-104 is the sole mitigation (explicitly Inc-6 scope, lifted Inc 7+). | test: mvn test -pl simulation -Dtest=VonTransportFilterTest (verify exists; if not, add) — assert createFilter rejects oversize array/deep graph. | approach: Append resource caps to PATTERN string before '!*', e.g. 'maxbytes=N;maxarray=N;maxdepth=N;maxrefs=N;' sized to the largest legit GhostSync/JoinResponse payload (measure a realistic TransportVonMessage with full neighbor list). title: [simulation] Split rollback orphans entities: grid bubble removed but accountant entity moves never reversed
description:
simulation/src/main/java/com/hellblazer/luciferase/simulation/topology/TopologyExecutor.java:248-262, 323-332, 395-426
Severity: High | Category: serialization-silent-data-loss

On a SplitProposal, BubbleSplitter.execute() relocates entities to the new bubble via accountant.moveBetweenBubbles() (BubbleSplitter.java:265) and adds the bubble to the grid (recordBubbleAdded). If a later executor-level check fails (accountant.validate() at TopologyExecutor.java:325 or the conservation check at :335), rollback() is invoked. rollback() only undoes GridOperations: BubbleAdded.undo (GridOperation.java:75-81) calls grid.removeBubble(newBubbleId). It does NOT reverse the accountant entity moves (explicitly documented limitation, TopologyExecutor.java:387-391 / 424-425). Result: entities remain assigned to newBubbleId in the EntityAccountant while the grid no longer has that bubble — they are spatially unreachable (getBubbleById returns null) yet still counted by getTotalEntityCount()/getDistribution(). getTotalEntityCount() therefore still equals totalBefore, so the post-rollback state silently 'passes' numerically while entities are orphaned. The reassuring log line 'EntityAccountant ensures entity tracking consistency - no entities lost' is misleading: tracking is consistent, spatial reachability is not. This is an RDR-004-class success-while-losing-data defect.

Fix: Make rollback reverse the accountant entity movements, not just grid structure. Capture the per-entity source/target bubble assignments performed during the operation and replay them in reverse (accountant.moveBetweenBubbles back to source) before/after removing the bubble, OR keep the bubble in the grid until accountant state is restored. At minimum, after a split rollback, move every entity assigned to newBubbleId back to sourceBubbleId in the accountant so no entity references a removed bubble. Add a test that fails the executor-level validate() after a successful splitter run and asserts every entity resolves to a live grid bubble.

Verify evidence: Confirmed by reading the cited code. BubbleSplitter.execute() relocates entities via accountant.moveBetweenBubbles() and grid.addBubble()+recordBubbleAdded() (BubbleSplitter.java:251-252, 265). TopologyExecutor.rollback() (TopologyExecutor.java:395-426) only iterates operationHistory and calls operation.undo(bubbleGrid); for BubbleAdded.undo (GridOperation.java:74-81) that is solely grid.removeBubble(bubbleId). No accountant.moveBetweenBubbles is ever reversed — confirmed by the explicit limitation docstring (TopologyExecutor.java:387-391) and the log line at 424-425. getTotalEntityCount() reads accountant.getDistribution() (TopologyExecutor.java:433-434), which is purely accountant-backed (EntityAccountant.java:217-228) and continues to count entities under newBubbleId after the grid bubble is removed. So on the validate()-failure rollback path (line 326-327), entities remain assigned to a bubble that getBubbleById now returns null for (spatially unreachable) while getTotalEntityCount() still equals totalBefore — the post-rollback state passes numerically. The 'no entities lost' log (line 425) is accurate about accountant tracking but misleading about spatial reachability, exactly
notes: ENRICHED 2026-06-04 | still-valid: yes | anchors: TopologyExecutor.java:244 splitter.execute(split), :325-332 accountant.validate() -> rollback on fail, :334-341 entity-count mismatch -> rollback, :395-426 rollback() body. rollback only replays GridOperation.undo (:415); :387-391 + :424-425 explicitly document 'Entity movements within bubbles are NOT reversed' and log misleading 'no entities lost' at :425. takeSnapshot() at :366-375 already captures per-bubble entity sets via accountant.entitiesInBubble — the data needed to reverse is ALREADY captured but unused in rollback. | test: mvn test -pl simulation -Dtest=TopologyExecutorTest (extend; add a split that passes splitter but fails executor-level validate, assert every entity resolves to a live grid bubble). | approach: Use the existing snapshot in rollback() to restore accountant state: for each entity now assigned to a bubble not in snapshot (the orphaned newBubbleId), move it back to its snapshot source bubble via accountant.moveBetweenBubbles before/independent of grid undo. Simplest correct form: diff current accountant distribution against snapshot and replay reverse moves so post-rollback distribution == snapshot. | acceptance: (1) after a split rollback, getBubbleById resolves for every entity (no entity references removed newBubbleId); (2) accountant distribution after rollback equals takeSnapshot() distribution; (3) the misleading :425 log line corrected or removed; (4) new regression test fails on current code, passes after fix. | blast-radius: rollback() is private, called from 3 sites (:248 split, :272 merge, :294 move). Fix must be conservative for all three — merge/move also relocate entities (BubbleMerger, BubbleMover). snapshot already passed in but currently only logged. title: [misc] GPUBufferPool pools no GPU memory — PooledBuffer is pure byte-accounting with no cl_mem/MemorySegment handle
description:
/Users/hal.hildebrand/git/Luciferase/render/src/main/java/com/hellblazer/luciferase/esvo/gpu/GPUBufferPool.java:46-59, 137-183, 191-213
Severity: High | Category: hollow-abstraction / wrong abstraction

The class is documented as a 'Buffer pool for GPU memory allocation' that reduces 'allocation overhead and fragmentation'. But PooledBuffer (46-59) carries only id, sizeBytes, sizeClass, timestamps — no cl_mem long, no ByteBuffer, no MemorySegment. allocate()/release() only mutate AtomicLong counters and a free-list of metadata records; no actual GPU buffer is ever created, reused, or freed. 'Reuse from free pool' (149-160) discards the reused record entirely and mints a fresh UUID, so even the metadata isn't reused — the hit just avoids incrementing missCount. Callers believing they obtained a reusable GPU buffer get nothing usable; the eviction/LRU logic operates on phantom bytes. This is an abstraction that simulates pooling without pooling.

Fix: Either store and return a real handle (cl_mem from clCreateBuffer or an FFM MemorySegment) in PooledBuffer and free it on eviction (clReleaseMemObject), or downgrade the class to an explicitly-named accounting/quota tracker and remove the 'reduce allocation overhead/fragmentation' claims so callers don't assume real buffer reuse.

Verify evidence: Confirmed by reading GPUBufferPool.java. PooledBuffer (lines 46-59) is a record of only {String id, long sizeBytes, long sizeClass, long allocatedAtNs, long lastAccessNs} — no cl_mem handle, no ByteBuffer, no MemorySegment, no native pointer. allocate() (137-183) only mints a UUID, mutates AtomicLong counters, and stores a metadata record in a map; it never calls any GPU/FFM allocation. The 'reuse from free pool' branch (149-160) does freeList.removeFirst() then discards the reused record entirely (only reads reused.sizeBytes() to decrement totalFreeBytes) and mints a fresh PooledBuffer with a new UUID — so even the metadata is not reused; the hit only avoids incrementing missCount. release() (191-213) and evictToMakeRoom() (328-346) likewise touch only counters and metadata lists; no native memory is ever freed. The class Javadoc (24-29) advertises 'Buffer pool for GPU memory allocation' reducing 'allocation overhead and fragmentation' — it pools no GPU memory and reuses nothing usable. This is a hollow abstraction simulating pooling without pooling. Severity held at High (not Critical) since no production consumer was verified and the defect is the misleading abstraction itself,
notes: ENRICHED 2026-06-04 | still-valid: yes | anchors: GPUBufferPool.java:46-59 PooledBuffer record carries only id/sizeBytes/sizeClass/allocatedAtNs/lastAccessNs — NO cl_mem long, NO ByteBuffer, NO MemorySegment. :137-183 allocate() only mutates AtomicLong counters + free-list of metadata records. :149-160 'reuse' path: removeFirst() from free list, discards 'reused', mints fresh UUID (:143) and new PooledBuffer (:154) — even metadata not reused, only hitCount++ avoided. :191-213 release() returns metadata to free list, no GPU free. | test: mvn test -pl render -Dtest=F324GPUMemoryManagementTest (existing caller test); a real handle requires GPU/OpenCL so guard with dangerouslyDisableSandbox or assert accounting-only contract. | approach: Two options per bead. (A) Make it real: add a handle field (FFM MemorySegment, or cl_mem long via clCreateBuffer) to PooledBuffer, return it from allocate, reuse the actual segment on free-list hit (don't mint fresh), clReleaseMemObject/close on eviction. (B) Honest downgrade: rename to GPUBufferQuotaTracker / accounting tracker, strip 'reduce allocation overhead and fragmentation' from class javadoc (:40 area), keep counters as a quota gate. Pick (B) unless a real-reuse workload exists (matches RDR-012-style infrastructure-only discipline). | acceptance: if (A): free-list hit returns the SAME underlying handle (assert identity), eviction releases it, no leak; if (B): javadoc no longer claims buffer reuse, callers (GPUMemoryManager) updated to not assume reusable GPU buffer. | blast-radius: callers = GPUMemoryManager.java (main) + F324GPUMemoryManagementTest. Option A changes PooledBuffer record shape (breaks both callers' construction/consumption). Option B changes class name (rename via Serena, updates both refs).
close_reason: Fixed wave6 (bb9c1a81): GPUBufferPool->GPUMemoryAccountant honest downgrade (no real GPU pooling, byte-accounting only); false reuse claims stripped incl getMemoryAccountant rename + hitCount doc. Both gates passed (critic caught residual naming, fixed); F324 28/28.

title: [render] CPU applies BEY_NUMBER_TO_INDEX to childOrder values; GPU shader uses them directly — index-convention mismatch
description:
render/src/main/java/com/hellblazer/luciferase/esvt/traversal/ESVTTraversal.java:206-215
Severity: High | Category: GEOMETRY / CPU-GPU divergence

ESVTChildOrder.getChildOrder() returns values sourced from TetreeConnectivity.CHILDREN_AT_FACE, which the CPU traversal treats as Bey indices and converts to Morton via BEY_NUMBER_TO_INDEX[parentType][beyIdx] (line 215). The code's own comment (lines 203-205) admits the GPU shader's CHILD_ORDER literal consumes these same values DIRECTLY without the conversion, calling this 'a pre-existing inconsistency under review in Luciferase-waft'. If the CPU and GPU disagree on whether the table values are Bey or Morton indices, the two renderers descend into different children for the same ray, producing divergent images / wrong hits on GPU. This is exactly the centroid/childOrder index-space consistency hazard called out for this unit. The ESVTChildOrderShaderParityTest pins the byte values of the table but does NOT prove both sides interpret those bytes in the same index space.

Fix: Decide one canonical index space at the table boundary. Either (a) make ESVTChildOrder emit Morton indices (apply BEY_NUMBER_TO_INDEX inside computeChildOrder) and have BOTH CPU and GPU consume directly, or (b) keep Bey and apply the conversion in the shader too. Then add a parity test that exercises a real ray through both CPU and GPU paths and asserts identical hit node, not just identical table bytes. Resolve Luciferase-waft before relying on GPU output.

Verify evidence: Confirmed by reading the cited code and both consumers.

CPU side (ESVTTraversal.java:206-215):
  byte[] childOrder = ESVTChildOrder.getChildOrder(parentType, entryFace);  // line 206
  int beyIdx = childOrder[pos];                                              // line 211 ("This is a BEY index!")
  int mortonIdx = TetreeConnectivity.BEY_NUMBER_TO_INDEX[parentType][beyIdx];// line 215
The CPU explicitly converts Bey->Morton because (lines 213-214) "ESVTNodeUnified stores children in Morton order, not Bey order", then indexes node.hasChild(mortonIdx) and getChildVerticesFromParent(..., mortonIdx, ...).

GPU side (raycast_esvt.comp): the CHILD_ORDER[6][4][4] literal is documented (lines 63,74) as derived from ESVTChildOrder.getChildOrder. In the traversal loop:
  int childOrder[4] = CHILD_ORDER[parentType][max(0,entryFace)];  // line 731
  int childIdx = childOrder[pos];                                  // line 736
  if (!hasChild(node, childIdx)) ...                               // line 739 - raw value, no conversion
  getChildVertices(parentType, childIdx, ...)                      // line 745 - childIdx used as Bey corner index (getChildVertices switch: case 0 "corner at v0", etc.
close_reason: Duplicate of Luciferase-waft (full-build-review 2026-06-04 confirmed; canonical=Luciferase-waft)

title: [render] ESVTData.fromByteBuffers/fromByteBuffer silently drop far pointers
description:
render/src/main/java/com/hellblazer/luciferase/esvt/core/ESVTData.java:275-292
Severity: High | Category: SERIALIZATION SILENT DATA LOSS

fromByteBuffers() reconstructs ESVTData via the 6-arg constructor new ESVTData(nodes, contours, rootType, maxDepth, leafCount, internalCount) (line 291), which routes to the constructor that sets farPointers = new int[0]. There is no farPointers parameter or read path at all. Any tree large enough to need far pointers (the builder emits them for relativeOffset > 32767, ESVTBuilder line 763-784) that is round-tripped through these in-memory buffer helpers loses ALL far pointers. resolveChildPtr() then returns the raw 15-bit far INDEX as if it were a node offset (ESVTData line 177-183), silently producing corrupt child links / wrong geometry with no error. Same RDR-004 class: a success-returning converter that drops a whole data channel.

Fix: Either delete the lossy fromByteBuffers/fromByteBuffer helpers (file ESVTDeserializer already round-trips far pointers correctly), or extend them to accept and read a farPointers buffer and pass it to the 7-arg constructor. Add a round-trip test with a tree that actually contains far pointers and assert farPointerCount() is preserved.

Verify evidence: Confirmed by reading ESVTData.java. fromByteBuffers (lines 275-292) reconstructs via `return new ESVTData(nodes, contours, rootType, maxDepth, leafCount, internalCount);` (line 291) — the 6-arg constructor (lines 63-66) which sets `this(nodes, contours, new int[0], ...)`, i.e. farPointers = empty. Neither fromByteBuffers nor the legacy fromByteBuffer (lines 297-301) has any farPointers parameter or read path. So a round-trip discards all far pointers. resolveChildPtr (lines 177-183): `if (node.isFar() && farPointers != null && ptr < farPointers.length) return farPointers[ptr]; return ptr;` — with farPointers length 0, the `ptr < farPointers.length` guard fails for any far node, so it returns the raw far INDEX (node.getChildPtr()) as if it were a node offset. No exception, no log — silent corruption of child links/geometry for any tree large enough to emit far pointers. This is the RDR-004-class pattern: a success-returning converter that drops a whole data channel. Severity High is correct: silent data loss with downstream corrupt geometry. Minor caveats (do not invalidate): these are in-memory GPU-transfer staging helpers rather than a persistence/wire path, and the same helpers a

title: [render] Node-reduction benchmark never builds per-tile BeamTrees — the headline metric is fabricated
description:
render/src/main/java/com/hellblazer/luciferase/render/benchmark/NodeReductionComparator.java:111-128

The 30% reduction target (Phase5a5BenchmarkRunner.targetMet()) is validated entirely against this non-measurement. title: [misc] countNodes returns maxIndex+1, materializing a dense file for sparse octrees (memory blowup + silent zero-fill)
description:
/Users/hal.hildebrand/git/Luciferase/render/src/main/java/com/hellblazer/luciferase/esvo/io/ESVOSerializer.java:54, 140-148 (countNodes) and ESVODeserializer.java:41,131
Severity: High | Category: SERIALIZATION / resource

countNodes() returns indices[last]+1 (max index + 1), not the actual stored count. For a sparse ConcurrentSkipListMap-backed octree with a few high-index nodes, writeNodes loops 0..maxIndex writing a zero (all-empty) node for every gap (lines 163-176), and allocates a single nodeBuffer of nodeCount*12 bytes up front (line 159) -- a sparse octree with one node at index 1,000,000 allocates ~12 MB and writes a million empty nodes. Deserializer mirrors this (capacity = max(nodeCount*8+1024,100000), allocate nodeCount*12). This is a DoS/OOM amplification on a crafted/large-index file and conflates 'absent node' with 'empty node' on reload.

Fix: Serialize the actual (index,node) pairs (sparse format) or stream nodes in chunks rather than one giant buffer; cap/validate nodeCount against file length before allocating ByteBuffer.allocate(nodeCount*12).

Verify evidence: Confirmed by reading the cited code. ESVOOctreeData backs nodes in a sparse HashMap<Integer,ESVONodeUnified> (ESVOOctreeData.java:44); getNodeIndices() returns sorted keys (line 81). countNodes() returns indices[last]+1 = max index + 1, not the stored count (ESVOSerializer.java:140-148, with the explicit comment "Return max index + 1"). writeNodes allocates nodeCount*12 bytes up front (line 159) and loops 0..nodeCount writing an all-zero 12-byte record for every gap via the else branch (lines 163-176). So a sparse octree with a single node at index 1,000,000 produces nodeCount=1,000,001 -> a single ~12 MB buffer and ~1M zero-filled records written to disk. The deserializer mirrors this: capacity = max(nodeCount*8+1024,100000) (ESVODeserializer.java:41,61) and nodeBuffer = ByteBuffer.allocate(nodeCount*12) (line 131). It also unconditionally constructs a node "even if all zeros" (lines 145-147), so a gap-fill-zero is reloaded as a present empty node -- absent vs empty is conflated, an unconditional data-correctness defect. title: [misc] writeNode/readNode do a TOCTOU check on 'disposed' then touch nodeBuffer that dispose() concurrently frees+nulls
description:

title: [lucien] Morton encode/decode asymmetry produces wrong neighbor keys
description:
lucien/src/main/java/com/hellblazer/luciferase/lucien/neighbor/MortonNeighborDetector.java:139-185
Severity: High | Category: correctness/geometry

decodeCoordinates() decodes the morton code and then shifts coordinates UP by (maxLevel - level) into the level-21 coordinate space (lines 166-177). findNeighborsWithOffsets() adds cellSize offsets in that same level-21 space (145-147), then calls encodeMorton() which feeds those level-21-space coordinates straight into MortonCurve.encode((int)x,...) with NO compensating down-shift (182-185). The resulting morton code is encoded from level-21 grid units but the key is constructed with element.getLevel() (155). So the embedded code and the level are inconsistent and the neighbor key does not correspond to the geometric neighbor cell. Note isBoundaryElement() (101) uses MortonCurve.decode WITHOUT the up-shift, contradicting decodeCoordinates and confirming the two code paths disagree on the coordinate convention.

Fix: Pick one coordinate convention. Either keep grid-unit coords throughout (decode without up-shift, add +/-1 offsets in grid units, encode directly) or work in level-21 space and down-shift by (maxLevel-level) before MortonCurve.encode. Add a round-trip test: for a known cell, findFaceNeighbors then decode each result and assert coordinates differ by exactly one cellSize on one axis.

Verify evidence: Confirmed by reading the cited code. The encode/decode pipeline is asymmetric. decodeCoordinates() (lines 166-177) decodes the Morton code then UP-shifts by `shift = maxLevel - level`: `(long)decoded[0] << shift`, yielding coordinates in the level-21 (maxRefinementLevel) absolute grid. findNeighborsWithOffsets() (145-147) adds `offset * cellSize` where `cellSize = 1L << (maxLevel - level)` (line 142) — consistent with that level-21 space. But encodeMorton() (182-185) feeds those level-21 coordinates straight into `MortonCurve.encode((int)x, (int)y, (int)z)` with NO compensating DOWN-shift, and line 155 stamps the key with `element.getLevel()`: `new MortonKey(neighborMorton, element.getLevel())`. The encoded Morton bits therefore represent level-21 grid units while the key carries the element's (coarser) level — mutually inconsistent for any level < maxRefinementLevel (only harmless when shift==0, i.e. level==maxRefinementLevel). The neighbor key thus does not correspond to the geometric neighbor cell. The claim's corroborating point also holds: isBoundaryElement() (101) calls MortonCurve.decode WITHOUT the up-shift and compares raw coords against cellSize/maxCoordinate in raw-level

title: [lucien] updateVisibility is a non-atomic read-modify-write on ConcurrentHashMap state
description:
lucien/src/main/java/com/hellblazer/luciferase/lucien/occlusion/VisibilityStateManager.java:125-176
Severity: High | Category: concurrency

The class advertises thread safety via concurrent collections (line 42), but updateVisibility() does get (126) -> compute new state (131-162) -> updateStateInfo put (166) with no per-entity locking or CAS. Two concurrent calls for the same entity (e.g. a render-thread visibility update and createTBV's internal updateVisibility at line 210) interleave: both read the same currentState, both compute and write, and one transition is silently lost, including lost TBV removal/expiry accounting. Additionally createTBV stores the TBV (206) and only then calls updateVisibility(false) (210) in a separate step, so an observer can see state=HIDDEN_WITH_TBV with the TBV not yet present, or VISIBLE->HIDDEN_WITH_TBV set by the plain state machine (138) with no TBV ever created, after which the expiry branch (148-149) sees tbv==null and the entity is stuck in HIDDEN_WITH_TBV forever.

Fix: Use entityStates.compute(entityId, ...) so the read-modify-write is atomic per key, and drive TBV side effects inside that lambda or via a single guarded path. Add a concurrent test hammering updateVisibility on one entity from N threads and asserting transition count == observed transitions.

Verify evidence: Confirmed by reading VisibilityStateManager.java. (1) Non-atomic RMW: updateVisibility (lines 125-176) does entityStates.get (126) -> compute newState (131-162) -> updateStateInfo put (166->387) with no per-entity lock or CAS. The class advertises thread safety at line 42, but ConcurrentHashMap only guarantees per-operation atomicity, not compound RMW; two concurrent calls for the same entity interleave and one transition (incl. TBV expiry accounting at 152) is silently lost. (2) createTBV (187-216) stores the TBV at line 206 then calls updateVisibility(false) at line 210 as a separate step — an observer can see TBV-present-without-HIDDEN_WITH_TBV or the reverse. (3) Stuck-forever path is reachable: the VISIBLE case at line 137-138 sets newState=HIDDEN_WITH_TBV on any !isVisible regardless of TBV existence; updateVisibility is called directly by pruneExpiredTBVs (286) and is a public API, so a VISIBLE entity can become HIDDEN_WITH_TBV with no entry in activeTBVs. The expiry branch at 148-149 guards `tbv != null`, so with tbv==null it never advances to HIDDEN_EXPIRED — the entity is pinned in HIDDEN_WITH_TBV indefinitely. All three sub-claims verified against the actual lines. Sever

title: [misc] DAG deduplication keys on a 64-bit-truncated SHA-256 digest with NO collision verification
description:
/Users/hal.hildebrand/git/Luciferase/render/src/main/java/com/hellblazer/luciferase/esvo/dag/DAGBuilder.java:236, 247-257, 287-298
Severity: High | Category: SERIALIZATION_SILENT_DATA_LOSS / dedup correctness

computeSubtreeHashes() stores nodeHashes[nodeIdx] = hasher.digest(), and JavaMessageDigestHasher.digest() (JavaMessageDigestHasher.java:55-60) truncates the 256-bit SHA-256 to the first 8 bytes as a long. identifyDuplicates() then treats equal 64-bit hashes as identical subtrees (hashToCanonical.putIfAbsent(hash, nodeIdx)), and buildCompactedDAG() collapses every node sharing a hash into the canonical node (oldToNew[nodeIdx]=oldToNew[canonical]) WITHOUT ever comparing the actual subtree structure/descriptors. A single 64-bit collision between two structurally-different subtrees silently merges them, corrupting the DAG (wrong geometry, wrong child pointers) while build() reports success and a bogus compression ratio. This is exactly the RDR-004 class: ACK success while dropping/replacing data. By the birthday bound a 64-bit space starts colliding around ~5 billion subtrees, but adversarial or hash-weak input can collide far sooner, and there is no detection at all.

Fix: After hash bucketing, verify candidate duplicates by deep structural equality (compare child/contour descriptors and recursively the mapped child sets) before collapsing; OR key the map on the full byte[] digest, not the truncated long. Add a regression test that injects two distinct subtrees with a forced hash collision and asserts they are NOT merged.

Verify evidence: Confirmed by reading the cited code. JavaMessageDigestHasher.digest() (lines 55-60) computes a full SHA-256 via digest.digest() but returns only the first 8 bytes: `ByteBuffer.wrap(cachedDigest, 0, 8).order(ByteOrder.LITTLE_ENDIAN).getLong()` — a 64-bit truncation. DAGBuilder.computeSubtreeHashes() line 236 stores this truncated long as nodeHashes[nodeIdx]. identifyDuplicates() line 255 keys dedup solely on the 64-bit long (hashToCanonical.putIfAbsent(hash, nodeIdx)). buildCompactedDAG() lines 287-297 retrieves the canonical by hash and collapses duplicates (oldToNew[nodeIdx] = oldToNew[canonical]) with NO comparison of actual subtree structure/descriptors/children. So any 64-bit collision between structurally-different subtrees silently merges them, corrupting child pointers/geometry while build() reports success — a genuine silent-data-loss / RDR-004-class defect with no detection or fallback verification.\n\nDowngraded from Critical to High: exploitability is bounded. Truncating a collision-resistant SHA-256 to 64 bits means accidental collisions follow the birthday bound (~2^32 subtrees before meaningful probability), far above realistic ESVO node counts. No untrusted/adversary

Fix: after bucketing, verify candidate duplicates by deep equality (compare child+contour descriptors and recurse over mapped child sets) before collapsing oldToNew[nodeIdx]=oldToNew[canonical], OR rekey on full byte[] digest. description:

long timestamp = frameManager != null ? frameManager.getCurrentFrame() : System.currentTimeMillis(); then dynamics.updatePosition(position, timestamp). This is a direct System.currentTimeMillis() call in production code (clock-injection mandate violation — should use an injected Clock). Worse, the two branches produce semantically incompatible units: getCurrentFrame() is a monotonic frame counter (small integers), System.currentTimeMillis() is epoch milliseconds (~1.7e12). EntityDynamics.updatePosition computes velocity from delta-timestamp; depending on which branch ran historically, the same dynamics object can see a frame-count delta of 1 and an epoch-ms delta of thousands, producing wildly wrong velocities. Same defect at line 326.

Fix: Inject a Clock (Clock.system() default, setClock() for tests) and use clock.currentTimeMillis() for the no-frame-manager branch. More importantly, do not interchange frame numbers and wall-clock ms in the same field consumed by velocity math — pick one time base for dynamics (frame-based, or clock-based) and use it consistently across both branches.

Verify evidence: Confirmed verbatim at EntityManager.java:139 and :326: `long timestamp = frameManager != null ? frameManager.getCurrentFrame() : System.currentTimeMillis();` then `dynamics.updatePosition(position, timestamp)`. Two genuine defects: (1) Clock-injection mandate violation — direct `System.currentTimeMillis()` in production code (one of the 70+ sites tracked by active bead Luciferase-mt7hi). (2) Unit mismatch — `FrameManager.getCurrentFrame()` returns `frameCounter.get()`, a monotonic AtomicLong frame counter of small integers (FrameManager.java:28,53-54), while the fallback returns epoch milliseconds. The consumer `EntityDynamics.updatePosition` feeds these into velocity = `(current.timestamp - previous.timestamp) / 1000.0f` (EntityDynamics.java:131, javadoc line 83 explicitly says 'milliseconds'). So when frameManager is set, a per-step frame delta of 1 is divided by 1000 and treated as seconds, inflating computed velocity by ~1000x versus the intended ms semantics — wrong velocities/accelerations. The reporter's specific cross-branch scenario (same dynamics object seeing both a frame-delta of 1 and an epoch-ms delta in the thousands) is somewhat overstated since frameManager is norm

title: [lucien] Publication-order race on all TetreeLevelCache static caches (key written before value, no memory barrier)
description:
lucien/src/main/java/com/hellblazer/luciferase/lucien/tetree/TetreeLevelCache.java:165-170, 364-375, 130-136, 320-331, 148-153, 99-115
Severity: High | Category: CONCURRENCY

Every cache-write method writes the parallel KEYS[slot] array first, then the VALUES[slot] array, with no synchronization, no volatile, and no atomic publication (e.g. cacheTetreeKey L168-169 writes TETREE_KEY_CACHE_KEYS[slot] then TETREE_KEY_CACHE_VALUES[slot]; same pattern in cacheParentChain L134-135, cacheParent, cacheParentType, cacheIndex). The readers (getCachedTetreeKey L368-370, getCachedParentChain L324-326, etc.) compare only KEYS[slot]==key then return VALUES[slot]. Under concurrent access (these are static, shared process-wide, and tmIndex()/parent-chain walks are hot paths reached from the concurrent AbstractSpatialIndex), a reader thread can observe the freshly-published key but a stale or null value for that slot due to lack of a happens-before edge across the two non-volatile arrays. Result: getCachedParentChain/getCachedTetreeKey returns null (→ recompute, benign) OR a value belonging to a DIFFERENT (x,y,z,l,type) tuple that previously occupied the slot → wrong TetreeKey / wrong parent chain → wrong SFC keys and silent spatial-index corruption. Java arrays of references give no per-element visibility guarantees without a barrier.

Fix: Publish key+value atomically. Either (a) replace the parallel-array direct-mapped caches with a single ConcurrentHashMap<Long, V> (matches TetreeRegionCache which already does this), or (b) store a single immutable {key,value} holder per slot in a volatile/AtomicReferenceArray so the key check and value read see a consistent pair. At minimum make the VALUES arrays AtomicReferenceArray and write value-before-key with the key being the volatile publish point, and have the reader re-read the value after confirming the key (double-check).

Verify evidence: Confirmed by reading the cited code. All static cache writers publish key-before-value with plain (non-volatile, non-synchronized) array stores: cacheTetreeKey L168-169 (TETREE_KEY_CACHE_KEYS[slot]=key; then TETREE_KEY_CACHE_VALUES[slot]=tetreeKey), cacheParentChain L134-135, cacheParent L120-121, cacheParentType L151-152, cacheIndex L103-104. Readers do the symmetric plain reads: getCachedTetreeKey L368-370 (if TETREE_KEY_CACHE_KEYS[slot]==key return TETREE_KEY_CACHE_VALUES[slot]), getCachedParentChain L324-326, getCachedParent L305-307, getCachedParentType L347-348. These are static fields shared process-wide, reached from concurrent tmIndex()/parent-chain hot paths. There is no happens-before edge between writer and reader threads, so the JMM permits a reader to observe a freshly-written KEYS[slot] while still seeing a stale VALUES[slot] from a prior occupant of that slot (slots are key&(SIZE-1), so distinct keys collide; the value need not correspond to the observed key). generateCacheKey is a maskable hash (collisions possible), so a key match does not by itself guarantee a matching value -- the missing barrier is what makes the wrong-tuple value observable. Two outcomes: (a)

title: [lucien] findEdgeNeighborsAtLevel / findVertexNeighborsAtLevel / findVertexNeighborsAtFinerLevels are hollow stubs returning empty lists
description:
lucien/src/main/java/com/hellblazer/luciferase/lucien/tetree/TetreeNeighborFinder.java:392-413
Severity: High | Category: HOLLOW STUBS

All three private helpers allocate an empty ArrayList and return it with a 'This is a placeholder for the complex geometric calculation' comment (L395, L403, L411) — no traversal is performed. They are reached from the PUBLIC API: findEdgeNeighbors (L88) calls findEdgeNeighborsAtLevel for both the parent level (L127) and child level (L133); findVertexNeighbors (L274) calls findVertexNeighborsAtLevel (L327) and findVertexNeighborsAtFinerLevels (L334). A caller cannot distinguish 'genuinely no cross-level neighbor' from 'not implemented', so downstream balancing/ghost/collision logic that relies on complete neighbor sets gets wrong topology with no error.

Add a non-vacuous test asserting the exact expected neighbor count, not assertTrue(count>=0).

Verify evidence: Confirmed by reading the cited file. All three private helpers are hollow stubs: findEdgeNeighborsAtLevel (L392-397), findVertexNeighborsAtFinerLevels (L399-405), and findVertexNeighborsAtLevel (L407-413) each do `var neighbors = new ArrayList<...>(); /* This is a placeholder for the complex geometric calculation */ return neighbors;` with no traversal (placeholder comments at L395, L403, L411). title: [sentry] LandmarkIndex.walkToTarget returns null on hull-exit and uses non-robust orientation — can drop points that ARE inside the mesh

title: [misc] Pooled node reuse leaks stale childrenMask: default clear() never resets it
description:
/Users/hal.hildebrand/git/Luciferase/lucien/src/main/java/com/hellblazer/luciferase/lucien/SpatialNodeImpl.java:42, 64-71, 78-83, 173-195
Severity: High | Category: concurrency/state-corruption

SpatialNodePool.acquire()/release() reset a node via node.clear() (SpatialNodePool.java:98,193). The clear() default (SpatialNodeStorage.java:43-45) only calls clearEntities(); SpatialNodeImpl does NOT override clear(), so the protected `byte childrenMask` (SpatialNodeImpl.java:42) is NEVER reset on recycle. A node that had children (childrenMask != 0) is returned to the pool, then re-acquired for a brand-new spatial key. hasChildren() (line 151) then wrongly returns true and hasChild(i) (line 139) reports phantom children. Concretely this breaks AbstractSpatialIndex.cleanupEmptyNode (line 1470: `node.isEmpty() && !hasChildren(spatialIndex)`) — the recycled node will never be reclaimed even when empty, and any split/traversal logic that consults the child bitmask reads garbage from a previous occupant. This is silent spatial-tree corruption introduced purely by enabling pooling. Additionally `childrenMask` is a non-volatile, non-atomic byte mutated with read-modify-write (mask |= / &=) under the doc claim of external write-lock protection, but cleanupEmptyNode reads hasChildren() and the pool recycle path runs without that contract held.

Fix: Override clear() in SpatialNodeImpl to also reset childrenMask = 0 (and any subclass state, e.g. OcclusionAwareSpatialNode). Add a pool round-trip test asserting an acquired node has childrenMask==0 and !hasChildren() after a prior occupant had children.

Verify evidence: CONFIRMED by reading the cited code. (1) SpatialNodeImpl.java:42 declares `protected byte childrenMask = 0;`. (2) SpatialNodeStorage.java:43-45 default `clear()` only calls `clearEntities()`. (3) SpatialNodeImpl does NOT override `clear()` (verified — only clearEntities() at line 86-88 is overridden), so `clear()` never resets `childrenMask`. (4) SpatialNodePool.acquire() (line 98) and release() (line 193) both invoke `node.clear()`, which therefore leaves any prior `childrenMask` intact on recycle. (5) hasChildren() (line 151-153) returns `childrenMask != 0` and hasChild(i) (139-143) reads the bitmask — so a recycled node carrying a stale non-zero mask reports phantom children. (6) The cleanup-reclaim consumer is real: AbstractSpatialIndex.cleanupEmptyNode (line ~1470) gates on `!hasChildren(spatialIndex)`, and both Octree.hasChildren (Octree.java:529) and Tetree.hasChildren (Tetree.java:1998) resolve to `node.hasChildren()` i.e. the stale mask. So a recycled node re-inserted under a new empty key would never be reclaimed, and traversal/split logic reading hasChild(i) reads garbage. The defect mechanism is sound and `clear()` failing to reset the mask is a genuine bug.

Severity a

title: [lucien] Migration inserts null content yet counts the entity as successfully migrated
description:

Severity: High | Category: serialization-silent-data-loss

title: [lucien] Simulated cascading recovery is vacuous — Level 1 always succeeds, escalation logic is dead code
description:
lucien/src/main/java/com/hellblazer/luciferase/lucien/balancing/fault/CascadingRecoveryImpl.java:302-454
Severity: High | Category: test-gap

In simulated mode, attemptBarrierSync calls verifyRecovery (line 330), which calls handler.markHealthy(partitionId) then checks status==HEALTHY (lines 445-454) — this is always true because markHealthy just set it. Therefore Level 1 (BARRIER) always succeeds whenever validatePartitionState passes, so attemptStateTransfer and attemptFullRebuild are unreachable, the retry/backoff loop never runs, and the 'cascading' escalation that the class is named for is structurally dead. The simulation cannot exercise any failure/escalation path it claims to model, so any test asserting cascading behavior against this is vacuous.

Fix: Make verifyRecovery validate something independent of the action just taken, or inject per-level success/failure outcomes (deterministic seed/strategy) so state-transfer and full-rebuild paths and the retry backoff can actually be exercised. At minimum document that simulated mode only ever exercises Level 1.

Verify evidence: Confirmed by reading CascadingRecoveryImpl.java. verifyRecovery (lines 445-454) is self-fulfilling: it calls `handler.markHealthy(partitionId)` (449), then reads `var status = handler.checkHealth(partitionId)` (452) and returns `status == PartitionStatus.HEALTHY` (453) — true by construction since markHealthy just set it. attemptBarrierSync (302-353) returns success whenever validatePartitionState passes (314) AND verifyRecovery is true (330). validatePartitionState (435-443) returns true for SUSPECTED/FAILED, which is exactly the precondition canRecover (468) requires before recover is even invoked. So Level 1 BARRIER succeeds for any partition legitimately in recovery. The cascade driver executeCascadingRecovery (212-227) only escalates `if (!result.success())`, so since BARRIER always succeeds, attemptStateTransfer (355-393), attemptFullRebuild (395-433), the retry/backoff loop (255-288), and the escalation log path (225-226) are all unreachable in simulated mode. title: [misc] 3D Morton decode truncates the 63-bit code to 32 bits, corrupting any coordinate above ~10 bits
description:
/Users/hal.hildebrand/git/Luciferase/dyada-java/src/main/java/com/dyada/performance/MortonOptimizer.java:66-82
Severity: High | Category: CORRECTNESS / silent-data-loss

encode3D() builds a long Morton code using interleave21() that spans up to 63 bits (3x21-bit coords). But decodeX3D/Y3D/Z3D do `compact1By2((int) morton)` (line 67/74/81), narrowing the long to int and discarding bits 32-62 BEFORE de-interleaving. So any coordinate whose bits land in the upper 32 bits of the code (i.e. component values >= ~2^10 in any axis) decode to a wrong value. The encode->decode round-trip is therefore lossy and silent: no exception, just wrong coordinates. compact1By2 is also written for `int` (final mask 0x000003ff caps output at 10 bits), so even structurally it cannot recover a 21-bit component. decodeNormalized / MortonCache.decode3DCached propagate the corruption.

Fix: Make compact1By2 operate on `long` (use long masks covering the 0x...249 pattern across 63 bits and a final mask of 0x1FFFFF) and change decodeX3D/Y3D/Z3D to pass the full `long morton` (and `morton>>1`, `morton>>2`) without the (int) cast. Add a round-trip property test asserting decode(encode(x,y,z))==(x,y,z) for components up to 2^21-1, not just small values.

Verify evidence: Confirmed by reading the cited code. decodeX3D/Y3D/Z3D (lines 67/74/81) all call `compact1By2((int) morton)` — the `(int)` cast narrows the up-to-63-bit long Morton code (built by `encode3D` via `interleave21`, lines 43-47/109-117, which is correct full-long math) to its low 32 bits BEFORE de-interleaving. Axis-X bit k lands at Morton position 3k, so only positions 0-31 survive the cast: X bits 0-10 (bit 11 sits at position 33, dropped), similarly clipping Y/Z. Independently, `compact1By2` (lines 146-153) ends with `x = (x ^ (x >> 16)) & 0x000003ff;` — a 10-bit final mask — so the result is structurally capped at 10 bits and a 21-bit component can never be recovered even without the cast. Encode is lossless but decode is not, making the round-trip silently lossy (no exception, just wrong coordinates) for any component value above ~2^10. Both failure mechanisms claimed (int truncation and the 0x000003ff cap) are present. The title's '~10 bits' is accurate to the 10-bit final mask. Severity High is justified: silent data corruption that propagates through decodeNormalized3D and any MortonCache 3D decode path.

title: [lucien] Baumgarte stabilization bias has wrong sign — penetration correction opposes separation
description:
lucien/src/main/java/com/hellblazer/luciferase/lucien/collision/physics/constraints/ContactConstraint.java:99, 115
Severity: High | Category: bug

prepare() sets `bias = -BAUMGARTE_FACTOR * penetrationError / deltaTime` (negative for any positive penetration). solve() computes `lambda = normalMass * (-vn + bias)`. The convention here (relVel = velA - velB, positive lambda applied as +impulse to A separates A from B) requires a POSITIVE bias to inject extra separating impulse proportional to penetration depth. With the negative bias, deeper penetration REDUCES the corrective normal impulse — Baumgarte stabilization fights penetration recovery instead of accelerating it, and the clamp at line 119 (`max(0, sum+lambda)`) can zero it out entirely. Penetrating stacks will sink rather than recover.

Fix: Use `bias = BAUMGARTE_FACTOR * penetrationError / deltaTime` (positive), so `-vn + bias` adds restitution-like push-out. Verify against a single-contact resting-on-floor regression that penetration monotonically decreases over solver iterations.

Verify evidence: Confirmed by reading ContactConstraint.java. Line 98-99: `float penetrationError = Math.max(penetrationDepth - SLOP, 0.0f); bias = -BAUMGARTE_FACTOR * penetrationError / deltaTime;` — penetrationError is always >= 0, so bias is always <= 0 (strictly negative for any penetration beyond SLOP).

Line 115: `float lambda = normalMass * (-vn + bias);` with vn = relVel.dot(normal), relVel = velA - velB (lines 110-114).

applyImpulse (lines 165-171) applies +impulse to A and -impulse to B, so a positive lambda is the *separating* impulse. The clamp at line 119 `normalImpulseSum = Math.max(0, normalImpulseSum + lambda)` forbids pulling (no negative accumulated impulse).

For a penetrating contact near rest (vn ≈ 0), correct Baumgarte stabilization must inject an *extra separating* impulse proportional to penetration depth, i.e. lambda must increase with depth → the bias term must be POSITIVE under this (-vn + bias) / separating-positive-lambda convention. Instead bias is negative, so lambda = normalMass*(0 + bias) < 0, which the line-119 clamp zeros out. Deeper penetration therefore reduces (and via the clamp, eliminates) the corrective normal impulse rather than accelerating recovery. Pene

With relVel=velA-velB and positive lambda separating A from B, solve() computes -vn + bias; a positive bias adds push-out proportional to penetration depth. Negative bias currently shrinks the corrective impulse for deeper penetration and the L119 clamp can zero it. | acceptance: (1) for a body resting penetrated on a kinematic floor, penetrationDepth decreases monotonically across solver iterations; (2) at zero penetration bias==0 (no spurious push from SLOP-clamped error); (3) no energy injection on a resting stack (velocity converges to ~0). | blast-radius: ContactConstraint is a Constraint impl in collision/physics/constraints; prepare()/solve() drive the iterative solver. Verify other Constraint impls (DistanceConstraint etc.) and any solver loop using bias sign convention are unaffected -- this is a localized sign fix in one class.

title: [lucien-distributed] BalanceCoordinatorServer streamBalanceUpdates has no concurrent-session cap (connection-level DoS)
description:
lucien-distributed/src/main/java/com/hellblazer/luciferase/lucien/balancing/grpc/BalanceCoordinatorServer.java:198-227
Severity: High | Category: resource-leak

streamBalanceUpdates unconditionally creates a StreamSession and puts it in activeStreams for every inbound stream. Unlike GhostExchangeServiceImpl (which enforces MAX_ACTIVE_STREAMS=1024 and returns RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED, GhostExchangeServiceImpl.java:67,154-165), the balance server accepts unbounded streams, each pinning an activeStreams entry and spawning virtual-thread tasks per onNext (line 211). A hostile/buggy peer opening many cheap streams exhausts memory/threads. The RDR-013 connection-level DoS mitigation applied to ghost was not applied to the balance coordinator server, which exposes the same StreamObserver surface.

Fix: Apply the same MAX_ACTIVE_STREAMS guard at the top of streamBalanceUpdates, rejecting with Status.RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED once the cap is reached, exactly as GhostExchangeServiceImpl does.

Verify evidence: Confirmed by reading BalanceCoordinatorServer.streamBalanceUpdates (lines 198-227). It unconditionally creates and registers a session with no cap: line 202-204 `var sessionId = "stream-..."; var session = new StreamSession(...); activeStreams.put(sessionId, session);` — there is NO size check before insertion. The returned StreamObserver spawns a virtual-thread task per inbound message: line 211 `virtualExecutor.submit(() -> processStreamUpdate(session, stats));`. No RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED rejection path exists anywhere in this method.

The asymmetry the claim cites is real. GhostExchangeServiceImpl.streamGhostUpdates DOES guard, on the same StreamSession/activeStreams surface: line 67 `private static final int MAX_ACTIVE_STREAMS = 1024;` and lines 154-165 `if (activeStreams.size() >= MAX_ACTIVE_STREAMS) { ... responseObserver.onError(Status.RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED.withDescription("too many concurrent ghost streams").asRuntimeException()); return new StreamObserver<>(){...no-op...}; }`. The comment explicitly attributes this to RDR-013 / Luciferase-06ujn and describes the exact threat (many cheap streams pinning unbounded virtual-thread tasks + activeStreams entries → connection-level DoS)

design:
### connectTo() check-then-act race on ConcurrentHashMap — duplicate connection leak
- Location (verifier-confirmed): **sim:von/transport/SocketConnectionManager.java:84-91**
- Category: concurrency · unit=von-transport · flagged by expert
- Root cause: The idempotency check `if (clients.containsKey(remote.processId()))` followed by `clients.put(remote.processId(), client)` is not atomic. Two threads calling `connectTo()` concurrently with the same `processId` can both pass the `containsKey` check (both see `false`), both create a `SocketClient`, both call `client.connect()` (opening two TCP connections), and then race to `clients.put`. One connection ends up in the map; the other is leaked — it remains connected, consuming a socket and a background receive thread, and will never be closed by `closeAll()`. Under reconnect storms or multi-threaded join protocols this leak accumulates.
- Fix: Replace the check-then-act with an atomic `computeIfAbsent` pattern. Since `client.connect()` throws checked `IOException`, use `computeIfAbsent` with a separate tracking structure, or synchronize the `connectTo` method. A clean approach: `clients.computeIfAbsent(remote.processId(), id -> { var c = new SocketClient(remote, incomingMessageHandler); try { c.connect(); } catch (IOException e) { throw new UncheckedIOException(e); } return c; });`
- Verifier evidence: Lines 84-91 of SocketConnectionManager.java confirm the defect exactly as described. The guard at line 84 (`if (clients.containsKey(remote.processId()))`) is non-atomic with the `clients.put` at line 91. ConcurrentHashMap guarantees individual operation atomicity but not compound read-then-write sequences. design:
### Bubble.close() check-then-act race on volatile boolean — double broadcastLeave
- Location (verifier-confirmed): **sim:von/Bubble.java:380-385**
- Category: concurrency · unit=von-core · flagged by expert
- Root cause: The idempotency guard for close() uses a plain volatile boolean:
`private volatile boolean closed = false;`
with the guard:
`if (closed) { return; }
closed = true;`
This is a check-then-act pattern that is not atomic. ### SocketClient.close() is unsynchronized — concurrent close+send produces stream corruption on the receiver
- Location (verifier-confirmed): **sim:von/transport/SocketClient.java:142-149, 175-181**
- Category: concurrency · unit=von-transport · flagged by critic
- Root cause: `send()` is `synchronized(this)` but `close()` is not. A concurrent `close()` can set `connected = false` and call `socket.close()` while `send()` holds the lock and is mid-`writeObject`. The socket close interrupts the in-progress write, emitting a partial serialized object on the wire. The receiver will see either a `ClassNotFoundException` or `StreamCorruptedException` and tear down its input pipeline. Because `closeAll()` in `SocketConnectionManager` iterates and closes all clients concurrently with any in-flight sends, this race is reachable on any graceful shutdown while messages are in transit.
- Fix: Add `synchronized` to `close()`: `public synchronized void close() throws IOException { connected = false; ... socket.close(); }`. The brief hold of the send lock during close is acceptable — it ensures no partial write occurs.
- Verifier evidence: Lines 142-149: `send()` is `synchronized(this)`, acquiring the instance monitor before `outStream.writeObject(message)` and `outStream.flush()`. Lines 175-181: `close()` has no `synchronized` qualifier — it sets `connected = false` and calls `socket.close()` outside any lock. A thread calling `close()` concurrently with a thread mid-`writeObject` will close the underlying socket stream, causing the `ObjectOutputStream` to throw mid-serialization.

### WAL flush is not durable — PrintWriter.flush() does not fsync; crash between flush and process exit loses WAL record
- Location (verifier-confirmed): **sim:distributed/migration/MigrationLogPersistence.java:101-106, 131, 155, 179**
- Category: correctness · unit=migration · flagged by expert
- Root cause: The class Javadoc promises 'Atomic writes: Write to temp file, fsync, then rename to prevent corruption'. The implementation does none of this. It opens a plain PrintWriter wrapping an OutputStream, and calls writer.flush() after each write. flush() only pushes data to the OS page cache — it does not call fsync/fdatasync. If the process crashes after flush() but before the OS writes to disk, the WAL record is silently lost. The entity is removed from source but the PREPARE record never persists — crash recovery will not find the transaction and the entity is lost (orphaned with no record). Furthermore there is no temp-file-rename atomicity as claimed.

For full atomicity per the Javadoc claim, write to a temp file in the same directory, fsync, then Files.move with ATOMIC_MOVE. At minimum, force() is required for crash-safe WAL semantics.

### RealTimeController.stop(): Deadlock if Called from a TickListener
- Location (verifier-confirmed): **sim:bubble/RealTimeController.java:201-212**

- Root cause: stop() calls running.compareAndSet(true,false) then tickThread.join(1000). It never interrupts tickThread. ### Non-atomic double-buffer swap in FlockingBehavior and PreyBehavior
- Location (verifier-confirmed): **sim:behavior/FlockingBehavior.java:158-160**
- Category: concurrency · unit=behavior-spatial · flagged by expert
- Root cause: swapVelocityBuffers() performs two sequential volatile writes: `previousVelocities = currentVelocities; currentVelocities = new ConcurrentHashMap<>()`. Between those two assignments, a concurrently executing computeVelocity() thread reads `previousVelocities` and gets the same map that entities are actively writing to via `currentVelocities.put(entityId, ...)` (line 179). This collapses the double-buffer invariant: alignment reads and velocity writes operate on the same map for that window. The same bug is present in PreyBehavior lines 135-137. Declaring the fields `volatile` does not help — it only ensures visibility of reference updates, not atomicity of the two-step swap.
- Fix: Use an AtomicReference pair or a synchronized swap. Simplest safe fix: wrap both assignments in a synchronized block on `this`, and also synchronize the `currentVelocities.put()` and `previousVelocities.get()` callers against the swap. Alternatively, use a single `volatile int bufferIndex` toggle with a two-element array of maps; swap is then a single atomic int write.

### P2PGhostChannel.close() — event listener never removed (permanent leak)
- Location (verifier-confirmed): **sim:ghost/P2PGhostChannel.java:141, 227**
- Root cause: The constructor registers the event listener with `vonBubble.addEventListener(this::handleEvent)`. close() calls `vonBubble.removeEventListener(this::handleEvent)`. In Java, each evaluation of `this::handleEvent` produces a new Consumer instance; two instances created from the same method reference are NOT equal under Object.equals(). CopyOnWriteArrayList.remove() uses equals() and therefore never finds a match. The listener is never deregistered. After close(), the channel continues to process incoming GhostSync events, dispatching to handlers that may themselves have been cleared, producing ghost arrivals on a closed channel for the lifetime of the vonBubble.
- Fix: Store the listener reference as a final field: `private final Consumer<Event> eventListenerRef = this::handleEvent;` in the constructor body, then use `vonBubble.addEventListener(eventListenerRef)` and `vonBubble.removeEventListener(eventListenerRef)`. This ensures the same instance is passed to both calls.

### ObjectOutputStream not reset() between messages — unbounded memory growth on long-lived connections
- Location (verifier-confirmed): **sim:von/transport/SocketClient.java:64, 87-88, 142-150**
- Root cause: `SocketClient` reuses a single `ObjectOutputStream` instance (`outStream`) for the lifetime of the connection and never calls `outStream.reset()` between messages. `ObjectOutputStream` maintains an internal handle table that maps every serialized object to a back-reference. Each call to `writeObject()` adds entries to this table; none are ever removed. On a long-running simulation node sending thousands of `GhostSync` or `Move` messages per second, this table grows without bound, holding strong references to every `TransportVonMessage` and its `ArrayList<TransportGhostData>` — effectively a memory leak that will eventually cause `OutOfMemoryError` or severe GC pressure.
- Fix: Call `outStream.reset()` after each `flush()` in `send()`. This clears the handle table so serialized objects can be GC'd. For the common case where the same record type is sent repeatedly (e.g., `TransportVonMessage`), `reset()` causes the class descriptor to be re-sent on the next write, which is a minor wire overhead but correct and necessary. Alternatively, recreate the `ObjectOutputStream` periodically, but `reset()` per message is the standard pattern for long-lived Java serialization streams.
- Verifier evidence: Lines 87-88 create a single `ObjectOutputStream` for the connection lifetime. Lines 148-149 in `send()` call `outStream.writeObject(message)` then `outStream.flush()` with no `reset()`. Java's `ObjectOutputStream` maintains an internal handle table (`handleTable`) that maps every serialized object to a back-reference for cycle detection/deduplication. Each `writeObject()` call adds entries; nothing removes them without `reset()`. This is a real defect.

description: sim:bubble/BubbleDynamicsManager.java:265-302. After addAll+remap, unregisterBubble(smaller) clears entityBubbles entries that were repointed to larger. Fix: don't touch entityBubbles in unregister, or unregister before remap.
