Mirror canonicalize()'s snapshot discipline. Then the (maxChange > MAX_VERTEX_CHANGE) guard at :126 becomes live. | acceptance: 1) maxChange reflects real per-vertex displacement; 2) guard terminates early on divergence (add test driving an oversized move); 3) normal planarize convergence unchanged for a known polyhedron; 4) NaN guard still honored | blast-radius: planarize(Polyhedron,int) callers within portal mesh pipeline -- behavior change is early-termination only (was never triggering before), so existing convergent cases are unaffected

title: [portal] Edge.equals lacks null and type guards — ClassCastException / NPE in hash collections
description:
portal/src/main/java/com/hellblazer/luciferase/portal/mesh/Edge.java:52-57
Severity: Medium | Category: correctness / crash

equals(Object obj) immediately casts obj to Edge with no null check and no instanceof check. Edge is used pervasively as a HashSet/HashMap key (Mesh.getEdges() builds a HashSet<Edge> at line 149; Polyhedron.ambo/subdivide/quinto use Map<Edge,Integer>). title: [simulation] readLogFile silently skips every malformed line, not just a torn tail
description:
simulation/src/main/java/com/hellblazer/luciferase/simulation/persistence/WriteAheadLog.java:415-425
Severity: Medium | Category: serialization / data-loss

readLogFile catches parse failures per line and continues (log.warn + skip) for ALL lines, not only a torn final record after a crash. A single corrupted/truncated line in the MIDDLE of a rotated log (e.g. partial fsync, disk error) is silently dropped and recovery proceeds as if those events never happened, while readEventsSince/recover report success. This is the RDR-004 'ACK success while dropping data' pattern at the WAL read layer; there is no checksum or 'corruption detected' signal surfaced to the caller.

title: [misc] EntityStreamConsumer constructed with hardcoded Clock.system() in RenderingServer constructor
description:
/Users/hal.hildebrand/git/Luciferase/simulation/src/main/java/com/hellblazer/luciferase/simulation/viz/render/RenderingServer.java:103
Severity: Medium | Category: CLOCK INJECTION

The constructor (line 103-108) builds entityConsumer with a hardcoded Clock.system() rather than this.clock. The later setClock() (line 120) does re-propagate to entityConsumer, so this is recoverable IF setClock is called before start(). But it is a latent trap: any future code path that reads entityConsumer timing between construction and setClock (or that forgets to call setClock) will silently capture wall-clock time. The constructor field this.clock is itself Clock.system() at that point, so passing this.clock would be equivalent and remove the special-case hardcode that future readers must remember to override.

Fix: Pass this.clock to the EntityStreamConsumer constructor (or defer consumer construction to start() where the injected clock is known), so there is a single source of truth for the clock and no construction-time system-clock capture that depends on a later setClock to correct.

title: [misc] app.start() opens the listener and consumers before all WS-handler state is guaranteed published
description:
/Users/hal.hildebrand/git/Luciferase/simulation/src/main/java/com/hellblazer/luciferase/simulation/viz/render/RenderingServer.java:360
Severity: Medium | Category: CONCURRENCY

start() registers the ws('/ws/render') handler that captures regionStreamer (line 353) and authLimiters/clock, then calls app.start(config.port()) (line 360), and only afterwards starts entityConsumer (364) and regionStreamer (367). regionStreamer is a plain (non-volatile) field assigned at line 168 on the starting thread; once the Jetty acceptor is live at line 360, an inbound WS connection handled on a Jetty worker thread can invoke regionStreamer.onConnect before regionStreamer.start() (367) has run, and reads regionStreamer / viewportTracker without a happens-before edge to the writes in start(). title: [misc] sendBatch swallows per-ghost serialization failures and ACKs success; isConnected always true

title: [misc] STALE state is never reached: default staleness threshold == TTL (both 500ms) and stored state never transitions to STALE

title: [simulation] rollbackOnViewChange uses getResult (resurrecting) instead of getResultIfPresent, inconsistent with the zombie-future guard
description:
simulation/src/main/java/com/hellblazer/luciferase/simulation/consensus/committee/CommitteeVotingProtocol.java:239
Severity: Medium | Category: concurrency

handleTimeout was deliberately changed to use ballotBox.getResultIfPresent (line 200) to avoid resurrecting a fresh VoteState for a proposal a concurrent path already cleared (Luciferase-0frcy.92). rollbackOnViewChange still calls ballotBox.getResult(proposalId) at line 239. The snapshot is taken under viewLock, but recordVote's success cleanup (lines 173-180: completeIfQuorum then proposals.remove + ballotBox.clear) runs WITHOUT viewLock, so between the snapshot (line 228) and line 239 a vote can complete and clear the proposal. getResult then computeIfAbsent-creates a brand-new never-completed VoteState, completes it exceptionally, and clear()s it. The created future is unreferenced so it is currently harmless, but it is the exact resurrection pattern the timeout path was hardened against and is a latent zombie-future bug if any caller ever captures futures from the ballot box outside the lock.

Fix: Use getResultIfPresent in rollbackOnViewChange's loop, mirroring handleTimeout: skip proposals already cleared rather than resurrecting state. Add a concurrency test interleaving a quorum-completing vote with a view-change rollback for the same proposal.

title: [simulation] Event whose processor throws is removed from queue and tracker but counted as neither reprocessed nor dropped
description:
simulation/src/main/java/com/hellblazer/luciferase/simulation/causality/EventReprocessor.java:processReady catch block (processor.process failure path)
Severity: Medium | Category: silent-data-loss

In processReady, the event is poll()ed and removed from eventTracker BEFORE processor.process(event). On exception the catch only logs error and continues — the event is permanently gone (already polled/untracked), totalReprocessed is not incremented, and totalDropped is NOT incremented either. So a processing failure silently loses the event AND is invisible to the drop metric / isHealthy accounting that downstream code may rely on to detect causality-window loss. The force-process WARN path is covered, but the ordinary in-window process-failure path leaks the event with no metric.

Fix: On processor.process failure, increment totalDropped (or a dedicated totalFailed counter) so the loss is observable, and document/decide whether failed events should be requeued. Add a test where the processor throws and assert the drop/failure metric advances.

title: [misc] WAL recovery silently skips malformed entries, dropping in-flight transactions on crash recovery
description:
/Users/hal.hildebrand/git/Luciferase/simulation/src/main/java/com/hellblazer/luciferase/simulation/distributed/migration/MigrationLogPersistence.java:248-250
Severity: Medium | Category: serialization-silent-data-loss

loadIncomplete() wraps per-line parsing in catch (Exception e) { log.warn('Skipping malformed WAL entry...') } (lines 248-250). A PREPARE record corrupted or torn by a crash mid-write is silently dropped from the recovered set, so an in-flight 2PC transaction that needs rollback is never returned to the recovery path and the entity it was migrating is silently lost/leaked (no rollback, no commit). Because appendDurable fsyncs (line 123) only the very last line can be torn, but a single bad PREPARE line still defeats the exactly-once recovery the WAL exists to provide. Catching broad Exception also masks UUID/enum parse bugs that should surface as recovery failures.

Fix: Distinguish an unparseable PREPARE record (recovery-critical) from a malformed COMMIT/ABORT marker: on a PREPARE parse failure, fail recovery loudly (throw or surface to an operator-visible RecoveryState quarantine list) rather than swallowing. At minimum elevate to error and count quarantined entries so a dropped PREPARE is detectable.
notes: ENRICHED 2026-06-04 | still-valid: yes | anchors: simulation/src/main/java/com/hellblazer/luciferase/simulation/distributed/migration/MigrationLogPersistence.java loadIncomplete() — per-line try/catch swallows ALL parse failures with log.warn('Skipping malformed WAL entry at line {}'); PREPARE-state records (recovery-critical) treated same as COMMIT/ABORT markers | test: mvn test -pl simulation -Dtest=MigrationLogPersistenceDurabilityTest | approach: Cannot know phase before parse, but a torn final line is normal (crash mid-write) while a corrupt interior line is not. Distinguish: tolerate parse failure ONLY on the last physical line (truncated tail); for any earlier malformed line, fail recovery loudly (throw IOException) or surface to an operator-visible quarantine list on the returned RecoveryState. Track lineNumber vs total lines read. | acceptance: (1) truncated tail line still recovers prior PREPAREs; (2) corrupt interior line throws/quarantines rather than silently dropping; (3) test injects a mid-file corrupt PREPARE and asserts it is NOT silently absent | blast-radius: callers of loadIncomplete() (migration crash-recovery path); MigrationLogPersistenceTest + DurabilityTest

title: [misc] Client gRPC channel has no maxInboundMessageSize cap (DoS surface on responses)
description:
/Users/hal.hildebrand/git/Luciferase/simulation/src/main/java/com/hellblazer/luciferase/simulation/distributed/network/GrpcBubbleNetworkChannel.java:404-420
Severity: Medium | Category: security

getOrCreateChannel() builds NettyChannelBuilder.forAddress(...).usePlaintext().executor(...).build() (lines 416-419) with no maxInboundMessageSize. The server side is hardened via GrpcServerHardening.applyInboundLimits (line 114), but the client accepts peer responses at the gRPC default (4MB) with no explicit bound; a malicious or buggy peer can push large/streamed responses through every getOrCreateChannel-backed RPC. The server hardening was justified as DoS defense (RDR-013/06ujn); the client leg of the same path is left unbounded.

Fix: Apply a maxInboundMessageSize on the NettyChannelBuilder consistent with the server-side cap (factor into the same GrpcServerHardening helper, e.g. a channel-side applyInboundLimits).

title: [simulation] proposalResults grows unbounded for any proposal whose result is never queried
description:
simulation/src/main/java/com/hellblazer/luciferase/simulation/consensus/committee/CommitteeServiceImpl.java:53, 74-82, 135-139
Severity: Medium | Category: resource-leak

The unbounded-growth fix (Luciferase-zwyf2) is tombstone-on-READ only: entries are removed at line 139 inside getQuorumResult after a caller consumes them. Any proposal that completes successfully but whose getQuorumResult is never called (proposer crashed, fire-and-forget caller, lost RPC) leaves its AtomicReference<Boolean> in the ConcurrentHashMap for the entire service lifetime. clearResultCache() is documented test-only (line 152). Under sustained migration load with imperfect polling this is a slow leak; combined with finding #1, failed proposals are at least never inserted, but successful-unqueried ones accumulate.

title: [simulation] Even committee size produces a nondeterministic consensus result on a split tally
description:
simulation/src/main/java/com/hellblazer/luciferase/simulation/consensus/committee/CommitteeBallotBox.java:173-213
Severity: Medium | Category: correctness/determinism

committeeQuorum(n) = (n-1)/2 + 1. For an even committee (e.g. n=8 -> quorum 4), a 4-YES/4-NO tally has both options at count 4 >= quorum. completeIfQuorum (lines 197-211) picks via Ordering.natural().onResultOf(Multiset.Entry::getCount).max(...); with equal counts the tie-break is unspecified, so the completed result (YES vs NO) is nondeterministic and may differ between nodes — a consensus-safety hazard. In practice committee size comes from context.bftSubset() which is normally odd (2f+1), mitigating this, but registerCommittee accepts any committee.size() and nothing enforces oddness, so the invariant is undefended.

Fix: Either reject/round even committee sizes to the next odd value at registerCommittee, or make the tie-break deterministic and conservative (on a count tie, do NOT complete — fall through to timeout, or always resolve ties to reject). Add a test with an even committee and a perfectly split vote asserting a single deterministic outcome.

Conservative tie-break is lower-risk if committee size is externally fixed. | acceptance: (1) n=8 with 4/4 split yields deterministic result (reject or no-completion) across repeated runs; (2) odd committee behavior unchanged; (3) test asserts determinism over many iterations | blast-radius: completeIfQuorum/committeeQuorum private to CommitteeBallotBox; registerCommittee callers; CommitteeBallotBoxTest

title: [simulation] AnimationFrame.track() unconditionally self-recurses with no termination or stop condition
description:
simulation/src/main/java/com/hellblazer/luciferase/simulation/animation/VolumeAnimator.java:170-183
Severity: Medium | Category: concurrency

track() calls `this.track()` at line 180 unconditionally. Under the PrimeMover @Entity bytecode transformation this becomes a self-rescheduling event, but as written there is no termination condition, no shutdown flag, and the recursion is unbounded. If the @Entity transformation is ever bypassed (direct call, unit test on untransformed bytecode) this is infinite recursion / StackOverflowError. Statements after the recursive call (lines 181-182, lastActive/eventOverhead update) are also dead in the literal-recursion reading and only meaningful under event semantics, making the control flow fragile and transform-dependent.

Fix: Introduce an explicit running/stopped flag checked at the top of track() so the loop can be terminated, and document that track() relies on @Entity event rescheduling rather than literal recursion. Move the lastActive/eventOverhead updates before the reschedule so they execute under both interpretations.

title: [simulation] frameCount is non-volatile and incremented non-atomically despite documented thread-safe concurrent access
description:
simulation/src/main/java/com/hellblazer/luciferase/simulation/animation/EnhancedVolumeAnimator.java:71, 144, 162

title: [misc] Two-phase migration has no cross-bubble lock — read-add-remove can interleave with concurrent updates/migrations
description:
/Users/hal.hildebrand/git/Luciferase/simulation/src/main/java/com/hellblazer/luciferase/simulation/bubble/TetrahedralMigration.java:232-269
Severity: Medium | Category: CONCURRENCY

executeMigration reads the entity from srcBubble via getAllEntityRecords()/stream filter (lines 234-238), adds to dstBubble (line 245), then removes from srcBubble (line 249). There is no lock spanning the source and destination bubbles. BubbleEntityStore serializes mutations per-store, but nothing serializes the cross-store sequence. A concurrent updateEntityPosition on the source between the read (line 238) and the remove (line 249) is lost (the stale snapshot's position is what gets added to dst, then the source copy is removed). The javadoc claims 'entity loss is impossible (worst case: duplicate)', but a concurrent in-flight position update IS silently lost. The 'eventual consistency via DuplicateEntityDetector' mitigation only handles duplicates, not lost concurrent updates.

Fix: Capture the entity under the source store's mutation lock and remove-then-add atomically, or add a migration-level lock keyed by entityId so concurrent updateEntityPosition cannot interleave. At minimum, re-read the source entity immediately before remove and re-apply the delta, and add a concurrent test (update during migration) asserting the latest position survives.

title: [simulation] Cooldown reservation ABA token is the clock millis 'now'; same-tick concurrent proposals can collide on restore
description:
simulation/src/main/java/com/hellblazer/luciferase/simulation/topology/TopologyConsensusCoordinator.java:342-372, 394-408
Severity: Medium | Category: concurrency

tryReserveCooldown writes 'now' (clock.currentTimeMillis()) into each bubble's slot and uses that same 'now' as the ABA token in restoreCooldown (lines 394-408: revert only if current == written). Two concurrent proposals affecting the same bubble that read the identical clock millis (very likely under an injected TestClock that does not advance per call, or coarse wall-clock granularity) will both write the same 'written' value. If proposal A is approved and proposal B is later rejected, B's restoreCooldown sees current == written (B's own value equals A's) and reverts A's live reservation to B's prior — clobbering the winner's cooldown, re-opening the oscillation window this code exists to close.

Fix: Use a unique per-reservation token (e.g. an AtomicLong sequence or the proposalId) stored alongside the timestamp instead of the raw 'now' millis as the ABA guard. Store value as a (token, timestamp) pair so restore only reverts entries whose token matches this reservation.

Replace 'written' with a per-reservation unique token (AtomicLong seq or proposal.proposalId()) and store the slot value as a (token,timestamp) pair so restore reverts only entries this reservation actually owns. | acceptance: (1) two proposals on same bubble issued at identical clock millis -- loser restore does not revert winner; (2) restore is conditional on the unique token not on millis; (3) existing TopologyConsensusCoordinatorTest cooldown/ABA cases still green; (4) add regression test seeding TestClock to a fixed millis across two concurrent reservations | blast-radius: private methods, no external callers; CooldownReservation record + lastChangeTimestamps map value type change if pairing token+timestamp; getAffectedBubbles unaffected

title: [misc] SocketClient.connect() uses no connect timeout; close() leaves outStream unclosed
description:
/Users/hal.hildebrand/git/Luciferase/simulation/src/main/java/com/hellblazer/luciferase/simulation/von/transport/SocketClient.java:99-106
Severity: Medium | Category: resource-leak

connect() does new Socket(host, port) which blocks on the OS default connect timeout (can be minutes) and runs synchronously on the caller thread (send is synchronous, line 117). A hung/unreachable remote stalls the calling protocol thread. Separately, close() (lines 155-162) closes the socket but never closes/flushes outStream; while socket.close() releases the FD, the ObjectOutputStream wrapper is left dangling, and any buffered bytes are silently discarded rather than flushed-then-closed in a defined order.

Fix: Use socket.connect(new InetSocketAddress(host,port), connectTimeoutMs) with a bounded timeout, and in close() close outStream (which closes the underlying socket) inside try/finally to guarantee ordered teardown.

title: [render] FileChannel.read() return value ignored — short reads silently produce truncated/zero-filled node and table data
description:

title: [render] resolveChildPtr silently returns the raw far-index when far pointers are missing or index out of range
description:

title: [render] classifyDominantTetFace never returns a Z-axis face and aliases +Z onto face 0
description:

title: [render] propagateTypesTopDown hardcodes root type 0, silently overriding the key-derived root type used elsewhere

title: [render] computeMortonChildIndex throws on pyramid-rooted tets — builder cannot handle the production-live pyramid boundary path

title: [misc] OctreeGPUMemory is not AutoCloseable and relies on deprecated finalize() as its leak backstop
description:
/Users/hal.hildebrand/git/Luciferase/render/src/main/java/com/hellblazer/luciferase/esvo/gpu/OctreeGPUMemory.java:243-250, 29, 218
Severity: Medium | Category: resource-leak / lifecycle

The class owns native (memAlignedAlloc, line 73) and GL (SSBO) resources but only exposes dispose() (218) — it does not implement AutoCloseable, so it cannot be used in try-with-resources and callers must remember dispose(). Its safety net is finalize() (244-250), which is deprecated, runs on the finalizer thread (wrong GL context for nodeSSBO.close()), and is not guaranteed to run — making the 'memory leak detected' warning the only signal and an unreliable one.

Fix: Implement AutoCloseable with close() delegating to dispose(); remove finalize() in favor of a java.lang.ref.Cleaner registered at construction (and never call GL from the cleaner — only free the native buffer there).
notes: ENRICHED 2026-06-04 | still-valid: yes | anchors: OctreeGPUMemory.java:29 (final class, does NOT implement AutoCloseable), :73 memAlignedAlloc (native), :218-241 dispose() (synchronized, idempotent, frees nodeSSBO + memAlignedFree), :243-250 finalize() backstop | test: mvn test -pl render -Dtest=OctreeGPUMemoryTest (no such test exists — add one; cannot exercise Cleaner deterministically but can assert close()==dispose() idempotency and that try-with-resources compiles/runs) | approach: Make class implement AutoCloseable; add public void close() delegating to dispose(). Replace finalize() (243-250) with a java.lang.ref.Cleaner registered at construction over a static state holder that frees ONLY the native buffer (memAlignedFree) — never touch GL/nodeSSBO from the cleaner thread (GL is not thread-safe). Keep dispose() as the explicit GL+native path; the Cleaner is the leak backstop for the native buffer only. | acceptance: (1) implements AutoCloseable, usable in try-with-resources; (2) finalize() removed; (3) Cleaner frees native buffer only, no GL calls; (4) dispose()/close() idempotent and double-free-safe; (5) render module compiles and existing render tests green | blast-radius: referenced by ComputeShaderRenderer, ESVOApplication, ESVTGPUMemory (render/src/main) — all call dispose() which is retained, so adding close()+Cleaner is purely additive (non-breaking).
close_reason: Already fixed in a prior wave (verified Wave-21, 475e4b3d). .157 GPUPerformanceProfiler: Clock injected + setClock, zero System.currentTimeMillis/nanoTime, deterministic Clock.fixed test asserts injected timestamp. .162 OctreeGPUMemory: implements AutoCloseable (via bead .27), idempotent dispose() under write-lock + freed AtomicBoolean (double-close safe), finalize removed + Cleaner backstop, callers free it. title: [misc] SLF4J log statements use Python-style {:.2f}/{:.1f}/µs format specifiers that SLF4J cannot interpret
description:
/Users/hal.hildebrand/git/Luciferase/render/src/main/java/com/hellblazer/luciferase/esvo/gpu/profiler/GPUPerformanceProfiler.java:258, 313, 377
Severity: Medium | Category: logging-correctness

log.info("GPU baseline: {} rays in {:.2f}µs ({:.1f}K rays/ms)", rayCount, latencyMicros, throughput) and siblings (313, 377) use {:.2f}/{:.1f} placeholders. title: [misc] ESVOOpenCLRenderer advertises 'Far pointer support for large octrees' but uploads no far-pointer buffer and never wires one to the kernel
description:

title: [misc] getChildNodeIndexWithOctant existence test uses octant-shifted descriptor but sparse index uses unshifted mask -- inconsistent octant mirroring

title: [lucien] testOcclusionAtLevel index mismatch when buffer width is not a power of two
description:

title: [lucien] isPointInTriangle uses float barycentric test with no shared-edge tie-break — diagonal points classified inconsistently with fromWorldCoordinates
description:
lucien/src/main/java/com/hellblazer/luciferase/lucien/prism/Triangle.java:406-421
Severity: Medium | Category: GEOMETRY

contains() relies on isPointInTriangle barycentric test with inclusive a>=0&&b>=0&&c>=0 and a 1e-10f degeneracy guard. The class doc (lines 358-363) acknowledges a point on the y==x diagonal is contained by BOTH halves, but fromWorldCoordinates assigns y==x to S0 only. Float rounding in the barycentric computation near the shared hypotenuse means contains() can disagree with fromWorldCoordinates on which half owns a near-diagonal point, so insert (via fromWorldCoordinates -> S0) and a contains()-based query (matches S1) can land in different keys, silently dropping the point from range/containment queries. The two classification paths are not guaranteed consistent.

Fix: Make contains() apply the same y==x -> S0 tie-break convention as fromWorldCoordinates (or route both through one canonical classifier), and add a test sweeping points exactly on and epsilon-around the diagonal asserting insert-key == contains-match for both halves.

Add a test sweeping points on and epsilon-around y==x asserting insert-key (fromWorldCoordinates) == the half whose contains() returns true. | acceptance: (1) for points exactly on y==x, exactly one of S0/S1 contains()==true and it matches fromWorldCoordinates; (2) epsilon-perturbed points classify consistently; (3) existing TriangleTest/TriangleTmSfcTest green | blast-radius: contains() callers in prism PrismKey/Prism locate paths; isPointInTriangle is private (single caller).

title: [lucien] cellsQ() floors maxX/Y/Z but does not clamp to MAX_COORD grid bound, can encode out-of-range cells
description:
lucien/src/main/java/com/hellblazer/luciferase/lucien/sfc/SFCArrayIndex.java:143-167
Severity: Medium | Category: correctness

cellsQ computes grid-cell indices via Math.max(0, floor(queryBounds.max/cellSize)) but, unlike cellsQSimple (lines 192-194) and findIntersectingNodesForEntity, never clamps the upper bound to the valid coordinate range (Constants.MAX_COORD / 2^level cells). A query box whose maxX exceeds the domain produces cell indices >= 2^level; LitmaxBigmin then calls MortonCurve.encode on coordinates beyond MortonCurve.MAX_REFINEMENT_LEVEL bit width, producing aliased/garbage Morton codes and silently wrong (incomplete or spurious) range results rather than a clamped query. cellsQSimple clamps; cellsQ does not — an inconsistency.

Fix: Clamp minX..maxZ to [0, (2^level)-1] (cells) or to MAX_COORD-derived cell bound before calling LitmaxBigmin.computeIntervals, matching cellsQSimple. Add a test with a query box extending beyond the domain asserting cellsQ == cellsQSimple.

title: [lucien] estimateSFCRange builds a Morton range from raw AABB corners — interior in-sphere cells can fall outside [min,max]
description:
lucien/src/main/java/com/hellblazer/luciferase/lucien/octree/MortonKey.java:561-575
Severity: Medium | Category: correctness

estimateSFCRange computes only minMortonCode and maxMortonCode from the two AABB corner points (lines 561-562) and returns [min, max+1]. Morton codes are not monotonic along axis-aligned boxes (the Z-curve re-enters), so cells geometrically inside the sphere's AABB can have Morton codes < cornerMin or > cornerMax. Using a single contiguous [min,max] subMap for k-NN can therefore MISS valid neighbors. The class doc admits it is 'conservative (may include entities outside)' but the real risk is the opposite — false negatives in k-NN results. (Contrast LitmaxBigmin which correctly checks all 8 corners and produces multiple intervals.)

Fix: Either document and guarantee correctness by checking all 8 AABB corners for the min/max (as LitmaxBigmin does, lines 101-113) and ideally use the LITMAX/BIGMIN interval set, or have KnnSearcher fall back to a wider scan. Add a test placing entities at Z-curve re-entry positions inside the radius and assert they are returned.

Z-curve is non-monotonic so interior in-sphere cells can fall outside [min,max]. LitmaxBigmin checks all corners L101-113. | test: mvn test -pl lucien -Dtest=MortonKeyTest (also MortonKeyEdgeCaseTest); add knn-near-corner case | approach: Either compute true min/max over all 8 AABB corners (as LitmaxBigmin does) and ideally emit the LITMAX/BIGMIN interval set instead of one span, OR document estimateSFCRange as an over-broad candidate filter and have KnnSearcher widen its scan. Add a test placing a point that is in-sphere but whose Morton code is outside the 2-corner [min,max] span, asserting it is still found. | acceptance: (1) knn returns geometrically-correct neighbors near box re-entry zones; (2) test reproducing the missed cell now passes; (3) MortonKeyTest green | blast-radius: estimateSFCRange consumed by KnnSearcher subMap range (see classdoc L578+, RDR-008 P3); affects knn correctness for Octree/SFCArrayIndex.

title: [lucien] consecutiveIndex() cache: volatile long avoids torn read but benign recompute relies on undocumented determinism of two delegate caches
description:
lucien/src/main/java/com/hellblazer/luciferase/lucien/prism/PrismKey.java:146-174
Severity: Medium | Category: concurrency

consecutiveIndex() lazily fills volatile cachedIndex from triangle.consecutiveIndex() and line.consecutiveIndex(), each of which is itself a lazily-filled volatile cache (Triangle line 106, similarly Line). The pattern is safe ONLY because all three are pure deterministic functions of immutable state, so concurrent racing recomputes converge. This is correct but load-bearing and implicit: any future change making Triangle/Line indices order- or state-dependent silently introduces a publication-order race on the ConcurrentSkipListMap hot path (compareTo at line 354). No test pins the invariant.

Fix: Add a unit test asserting consecutiveIndex() is stable across repeated/concurrent calls for the same key and equal across equal keys, and add a comment cross-linking the three caches' shared determinism precondition so it is not silently broken.

title: [lucien] generateCacheKey hash path is lossy — full-key collision returns a wrong cached key for large coordinates
description:
lucien/src/main/java/com/hellblazer/luciferase/lucien/tetree/TetreeLevelCache.java:245-261, 364-375, 320-331
Severity: Medium | Category: GEOMETRY

For coordinates outside the small fast path (any axis >= 1024 or negative, L238), generateCacheKey collapses (x,y,z,level,type) into a 64-bit avalanche hash (L247-260). Readers such as getCachedTetreeKey (L368) and getCachedParentChain (L324) compare ONLY this hashed `key` (not the original coordinates) before returning the cached value. A 64-bit hash collision between two distinct large-coordinate tuples therefore yields a wrong TetreeKey/parent chain — silent wrong SFC result rather than a recompute. The fast path (L242) is collision-free (38 distinct bits packed into 64) so this only affects coords >= 1024, but those are exactly the deep/large-domain cases. Collision probability is low per pair but the cache is process-global and long-lived (1M-entry key cache), so over a long run it is a latent correctness hazard, not merely a perf concern.

Fix: Store the original coordinate tuple alongside the slot and verify (x,y,z,level,type) on read before returning the cached value (the hash is then only a bucket selector). Or switch to a map keyed by an exact composite key. The collision must devolve to a cache-miss (recompute), never a wrong-key return.
notes: ENRICHED 2026-06-04 | still-valid: NO -- already defended | anchors: TetreeLevelCache.java generateCacheKey L238-261 (fast-path pack for 0<=x,y,z<1024 L242, avalanche hash otherwise L247-260); getCachedTetreeKey L364-375 GUARDS with KEYS[slot]==key L368 returning null on mismatch; getCachedIndex L273+ same guard pattern. The hash is only a bucket selector -- a full-key collision returns a MISS, never another tuple's value. Existing TetreeLevelCacheKeyCollisionTest (rewritten under Luciferase-egjwk) asserts exactly this contract non-vacuously (same-slot different-key write -> evicted tuple reads own value or -1, never the other's). | test: mvn test -pl lucien -Dtest=TetreeLevelCacheKeyCollisionTest (passing) | approach: defect as filed (lossy hash returns wrong cached key) does not occur -- the slot is verified against the stored full key on every read. Original critique predates the egjwk read-guard fix. Close as already-fixed. | acceptance: n/a | blast-radius: n/a
close_reason: ALREADY FIXED (verified during full-build-review enrichment, still-valid=NO): TetreeLevelCache.generateCacheKey is already defended — the fast-path pack (0<=x,y,z<1024) + avalanche-hash fallback handles the case the bead flagged; no change needed.

title: [lucien] borrowArrayList(initialCapacity) may hand back a list already containing elements; ensureCapacity is misleading
description:
lucien/src/main/java/com/hellblazer/luciferase/lucien/internal/ObjectPools.java:45-49
Severity: Medium | Category: resource-correctness

borrowArrayList(int) borrows a pooled list and calls ensureCapacity(initialCapacity) (line 47). returnToPool only re-pools lists with size()==0 (line 143), so borrowed lists are empty in normal flow — but ensureCapacity on an ArrayList only grows the backing array, it never shrinks an oversized pooled array, so the 'capacity' contract is best-effort and a previously-grown pooled list can be much larger than requested (benign memory retention). More importantly, the pool is per-thread (ThreadLocal, line 29) but the borrow/return API is static with no ownership check: if a list borrowed on thread A is returned on thread B (e.g. handed across a CompletableFuture/executor boundary, which this codebase uses heavily), it lands in B's pool and A's pool slowly leaks — silent cross-thread pool corruption with no guard.

Fix: Document and ideally enforce same-thread borrow/return (e.g. tag borrowed lists with the owning thread in debug/assert builds and assert on return), or switch to the withArrayList(...) try-with-style API exclusively for call sites that cross thread boundaries. At minimum add an assertion in returnToPool that the returning thread owns the ThreadLocal pool.

Add javadoc on borrowArrayList/returnArrayList documenting same-thread-only, and in an assert/debug build tag the list with Thread.currentThread() on borrow and assert identity on return; steer cross-thread callers to withArrayList(...) (:82). | acceptance: javadoc states same-thread contract; assert fires on cross-thread return in -ea builds; ObjectPoolsKnnPoolingTest still green; no behavior change in normal flow | blast-radius: borrowArrayList(int) callers across lucien knn/collision/ray paths; withArrayList/withHashSet already provide the safe try-finally idiom

title: [lucien] Conversion swallows all per-entity exceptions into a warn log; caller cannot distinguish lossy from clean conversion
description:
lucien/src/main/java/com/hellblazer/luciferase/lucien/migration/SpatialIndexConverter.java:245-249

The per-entity catch (lines 245-249) records failedCount and an error string but migrateEntities returns void and octreeToTetree/tetreeToOctree return the target tree regardless of failedEntities>0 (lines 79/124). A caller receives a fully-constructed tree with no signal that N entities were dropped beyond a log.warn (line 256). title: [misc] lastBalancingTime is a plain non-volatile long read/written outside any lock in checkAutoBalance
description:
/Users/hal.hildebrand/git/Luciferase/lucien/src/main/java/com/hellblazer/luciferase/lucien/AbstractSpatialIndex.java:170, 1447-1462, 1786-1787
Severity: Medium | Category: concurrency

lastBalancingTime (line 170) is a plain `long`. checkAutoBalance() reads it and writes it (1453,1459) with no lock and no volatile, and is exposed via the BalancerHost facade (1786) so it can be invoked off the index's write-lock path. Concurrent callers can race on the rebalancing-interval gate (lost updates / stale visibility), permitting more-frequent-than-intended rebalances or torn reads. Also relies on System.currentTimeMillis() directly (1452) — covered by clock-injection bead mt7hi but reinforces the un-injected-clock+race combination.

Fix: Make lastBalancingTime volatile (or AtomicLong with CAS to enforce the interval gate atomically) and source the time from the injected Clock rather than System.currentTimeMillis().

title: [lucien] EntityCache put eviction TOCTOU and approximateSize drift under concurrent access
description:
lucien/src/main/java/com/hellblazer/luciferase/lucien/internal/EntityCache.java:82-95
Severity: Medium | Category: concurrency-race

put() does a check-then-act: if (approximateSize.get() > maxSize) evictOldest() then cache.put + conditional incrementAndGet (lines 84-92). Under concurrent puts the size check and the increment are non-atomic, so approximateSize can drift arbitrarily far from cache.size() (the documented 'approximate' is fine, but the drift directly gates eviction). evictOldest (lines 132-139) decrements approximateSize once per removed entry while other threads concurrently put — the counter can go negative or stay above maxSize, defeating the size cap (unbounded growth) or over-evicting. getStats() (line 117/158) reports cache.size() for size but hits/misses are read non-atomically across three AtomicIntegers, so the snapshot is not a consistent point-in-time view.

Fix: Drive eviction off cache.size() (or mappingCount) directly rather than a separately-maintained counter, or use an atomic compute/merge for the increment. Bound eviction in a loop until cache.size() <= maxSize. For getStats, accept the documented approximation but note it; the load-bearing fix is making the size cap actually hold under concurrency.
notes: ENRICHED 2026-06-04 | still-valid: yes | anchors: EntityCache.java put() check-then-act at :83-95 (approximateSize.get()>maxSize -> evictOldest at :85-87, then cache.put + conditional incrementAndGet at :90-93); getStats reports cache.size() at :118 while eviction is driven off approximateSize | test: mvn test -pl lucien -Dtest=EntityCacheConcurrencyTest (NONE exists — add one; no dedicated EntityCache test in repo) | approach: the size check and the increment are non-atomic so concurrent puts drift approximateSize relative to cache.size(), and the single evictOldest() (bulk ~25% removal, NOT LRU per class javadoc :29-33) is not bounded so size can transiently exceed maxSize. Drive eviction off cache.size()/mappingCount() directly and drop the separate counter, looping evictOldest() until cache.size()<=maxSize; getStats already uses cache.size() so it becomes consistent once the counter is removed. | acceptance: no approximateSize drift (or counter removed); eviction loops until cache.size()<=maxSize; concurrent-put test shows size stays bounded; getStats consistent with cache.size() | blast-radius: EntityCache.put/remove/clear/getStats consumers (entity bounds/position caching in lucien internal); behavior already documented non-LRU (Luciferase-lsy13)
close_reason: Fixed wave12 (3878c145): EntityCache single-source-of-truth (ConcurrentHashMap.size, removed desyncing approximateSize). Both gates passed (critic verified read-through cache, entityManager authoritative, bulk-eviction never loses data); EntityCacheConcurrencyTest.

title: [misc] NavigableSet impl returns stale lazily-cached sortedView; modificationCount/SORT_THRESHOLD dead; class effectively unused
description:
/Users/hal.hildebrand/git/Luciferase/lucien/src/main/java/com/hellblazer/luciferase/lucien/SpatialIndexSet.java:297-316, 180-195, 34, 43
Severity: Medium | Category: concurrency/dead-code

SpatialIndexSet implements NavigableSet and is advertised as a high-performance ConcurrentSkipList replacement, but: (1) all navigation ops (ceiling/floor/first/last/iterator/subSet...) read getSortedView(), a snapshot ConcurrentSkipListSet rebuilt only when sortedView==null. Between an add()/remove() that nulls it and the next rebuild there is a window where two callers observe inconsistent views, and pollFirst/pollLast (180-195) read the snapshot then remove() from primary — TOCTOU that can return an element already removed by another thread or fail to poll a present element. (2) modificationCount (line 43, plain long) is incremented in invalidateSortedView() outside any lock and SORT_THRESHOLD (line 34) is never read — dead machinery implying a re-sort policy that does not exist. A symbol scan shows the only non-self reference is a javadoc mention in SpatialKey.java, so the class is not wired into the live index — a public, partially-broken, untested abstraction.

Fix: Either delete SpatialIndexSet (it is unused) or, if intended for use, back navigation directly with a ConcurrentSkipListSet and remove the lazy-snapshot + dead modificationCount/SORT_THRESHOLD logic; make pollFirst/pollLast atomic. Add concurrency tests before wiring it in.

title: [misc] release()/acquire() size accounting is TOCTOU: pool can exceed maxSize and currentSize can drift
description:
/Users/hal.hildebrand/git/Luciferase/lucien/src/main/java/com/hellblazer/luciferase/lucien/SpatialNodePool.java:185-204, 86-109
Severity: Medium | Category: concurrency

release() does `int size = currentSize.get(); if (size < maxSize) { pool.offer(node); currentSize.incrementAndGet(); }` (190-196). The get-then-increment is not atomic, so N concurrent releasers can all observe size==maxSize-1 and each offer+increment, pushing the queue and currentSize above maxSize (unbounded growth defeating the cap). Symmetrically acquire() polls then decrements currentSize separately (87-95); a poll() that loses a race can leave currentSize and the actual queue length inconsistent. The cap is advisory only, undermining the memory-bound guarantee the pool advertises.

Fix: Make the cap atomic: CAS-loop on currentSize (only offer when incrementAndGet result <= maxSize, else undo) or derive size from pool.size() consistently. At minimum bound the offer with an atomic compare to maxSize.

Make it atomic: CAS-loop on currentSize (offer only when incrementAndGet()<=maxSize, else decrement-undo and drop the node to GC), or derive size consistently from pool.size(). Apply the symmetric fix to acquire so currentSize tracks pool occupancy. | acceptance: under concurrent releasers pool.size() never exceeds maxSize and currentSize never drifts from actual occupancy; SpatialNodePoolIntegrationTest green; new concurrency test passes | blast-radius: release()/acquire()/releaseAll (:209) and grow()/preAllocate (:137/:164) all read-modify currentSize; getStats (:129) reports currentSize.get(); used by spatial node lifecycle in lucien

title: [sentry] circumsphereRadius uses centerSphereFast (float, non-adaptive) for Delaunay validation
description:

title: [sentry] rebuild and track silently drop points whose locate returns null
description:
sentry/src/main/java/com/hellblazer/sentry/MutableGrid.java:229-281 (rebuildOptimized) and 308-320 (track with near)

title: [misc] validateRefinementDecisions only inspects dimension 0 of each LevelIndex despite a multi-dimensional level model
description:
/Users/hal.hildebrand/git/Luciferase/dyada-java/src/main/java/com/dyada/refinement/GradientBasedRefinement.java:164-187
Severity: Medium | Category: CORRECTNESS / silent-scope-reduction

validateRefinementDecisions() iterates all decisions but reads `cellIndex.getLevel(0)` (lines 174, 179) — hard-coded dimension 0 — to enforce max/min level constraints. LevelIndex is per-dimension (byte[] levels), so a cell refined deeply in dimensions 1..n-1 but shallow in dimension 0 will pass validation even when it exceeds getMaxRefinementLevel() in another axis, and conversely a min-level COARSEN can be wrongly rejected/accepted. The Javadoc also promises 'smooth transitions between refinement levels' but the body only does a per-cell level-bound check and never compares neighboring cells, so the advertised 2:1-balance / smoothness validation is not implemented (hollow vs documented contract).

Fix: Check the level across all dimensions (e.g. max over getLevel(d) for d in [0,dimensions)) for the REFINE/COARSEN bound, and either implement the documented neighbor-smoothness check or correct the Javadoc to state only level bounds are validated.

title: [misc] mortonDistance2D returns 0 for identical codes and is a quadtree-LCA depth, not a distance
description:
/Users/hal.hildebrand/git/Luciferase/dyada-java/src/main/java/com/dyada/performance/MortonOptimizer.java:196-198
Severity: Medium | Category: CORRECTNESS

mortonDistance2D computes Long.numberOfTrailingZeros(morton1 ^ morton2)/2. For equal codes xor==0, numberOfTrailingZeros(0)==64, returning 32 (a large 'distance' for identical points) — the inverse of intended proximity semantics. For differing codes it returns the level at which the codes first diverge (shared-prefix length), which is a quadtree common-ancestor depth, not a spatial/Euclidean or even Chebyshev distance, so 'spatial proximity queries' built on it will rank incorrectly (two points in adjacent cells across a major quadrant boundary score as very far).

Fix: Special-case equal codes to 0. Rename/redefine to clarify it is shared-prefix depth, or decode and compute an actual coordinate distance. Add tests covering equal codes and the cross-quadrant-adjacency case.

title: [common] addAll(FloatArrayList) grows backing array to exact newSize — O(n^2) on repeated appends
description:
common/src/main/java/com/hellblazer/luciferase/common/FloatArrayList.java:88-95
Severity: Medium | Category: Performance / latent

title: [misc] composeWithLinear allocates result matrix with wrong column count for non-square composition
description:
/Users/hal.hildebrand/git/Luciferase/dyada-java/src/main/java/com/dyada/transformations/LinearTransformation.java:416
Severity: Medium | Category: CORRECTNESS

composeWithLinear computes result = other.matrix * this.matrix and allocates `new double[other.targetDimension][targetDimension]` (line 416), then iterates j over [0,targetDimension) writing result[i][j] = sum_k other[i][k]*this[k][j]. The product other(p x q) * this(q x r) is p x r where r = this.sourceDimension, NOT this.targetDimension. For non-square `this` (sourceDimension != targetDimension) this both over/under-sizes the result and indexes matrix[k][j] with j ranging over targetDimension while the valid column range of `this` is sourceDimension -> ArrayIndexOutOfBounds or wrong/missing columns. Only correct by accident for square matrices, which is why tests likely pass.

Fix: Allocate `new double[other.targetDimension][sourceDimension]` and iterate j over [0,sourceDimension). Add a non-square composition test (e.g. 3x2 composed with 2x3).
notes: ENRICHED 2026-06-04 | still-valid: yes | anchors: dyada-java/src/main/java/com/dyada/transformations/LinearTransformation.java composeWithLinear:408-428. Bug at 416: new double[other.targetDimension][targetDimension] and inner loop 419 j<targetDimension. result=other.matrix(other.targetDim x other.sourceDim) * this.matrix(targetDim x sourceDim); guard at 409 requires sourceDimension==other.targetDimension. Correct result shape is other.targetDimension x this.sourceDimension; k runs over this.targetDimension (the contraction index = other.sourceDimension). | test: mvn test -pl dyada-java -Dtest=LinearTransformationTest | approach: The column count and k-range are wrong for non-square. result rows = other.targetDimension; columns = this.sourceDimension; contraction k over [0, this.targetDimension) (== other.sourceDimension by the guard). Allocate new double[other.targetDimension][sourceDimension], iterate j over [0,sourceDimension), k over [0,targetDimension): result[i][j]+=other.matrix[i][k]*matrix[k][j]. NOTE the bead's stated k-bound (sourceDimension) is itself off — verify against guard semantics: matrix[k][j] needs k in this's row range = targetDimension. Add a non-square test (e.g. 3x2 composed with 2x3 -> 2x2, and 2x3 with 3x2). | acceptance: (1) non-square compose produces correctly-shaped result without ArrayIndexOutOfBounds; (2) square case unchanged; (3) new non-square test green; (4) result equals hand-computed matrix product | blast-radius: composeWithLinear is private, single caller compose() at line 150; no external API change
close_reason: Fixed wave11 (9dd18632): LinearTransformation.composeWithLinear correct result dims + loop contraction + COMPATIBILITY GUARD (targetDim==other.sourceDim). title: [lucien] shouldMerge uses a hardcoded parent capacity (always 100), ignoring actual maxEntitiesPerNode

title: [common] OpenAddressingSet is non-thread-safe with mutable iterator capture of `table` field — undocumented and footgun-prone in a concurrent codebase
description:
common/src/main/java/com/hellblazer/luciferase/common/OpenAddressingSet.java:26, 31-33, 44, 105-144
Severity: Medium | Category: Concurrency / API contract

Fields `table`, `size`, `load` are plain (non-volatile) mutable state with no synchronization. The class Javadoc is empty and gives no thread-safety contract. In a library whose CLAUDE.md emphasizes ConcurrentSkipListMap/COW for shared spatial state, an unguarded open-addressing set used in spatial dedup paths is a latent race. AbstractSet's default iterator-fail-fast is also absent.

Fix: Document explicitly that the class is NOT thread-safe and is single-thread/externally-synchronized only; OR add a modCount and fail-fast check in the iterator so concurrent structural modification throws ConcurrentModificationException instead of silently corrupting iteration.

Fields stay non-volatile (single-thread contract). | acceptance: (1) class Javadoc documents threading contract; (2) if modCount added, iterating after a structural mod throws CME; (3) existing OpenAddressingSetTest still green | blast-radius: referenced only by IdentitySet.java and OaHashSet.java (same package, common module) + its own test

title: [lucien] SimpleFaultHandler has no Clock injection — all timestamps use System.currentTimeMillis() directly

title: [lucien] CascadingRecoveryImpl owns an ExecutorService but is not AutoCloseable
description:

title: [lucien] CCD broad-phase seeds kNN only from the start position, missing collisions along long sweeps
description:
lucien/src/main/java/com/hellblazer/luciferase/lucien/collision/CollisionSystem.java:419-429
Severity: Medium | Category: bug

processCCDForEntity builds the candidate set via `kNearestNeighbors(startPos, 100, searchRadius)` centered on the START position only, with searchRadius = sweepLength + buffer. A fast entity whose endpoint is far from startPos can collide with an obstacle near the END of its path that lies outside a sphere of radius (sweepLength+buffer) centered at start — e.g. an obstacle just past the endpoint is at distance ~sweepLength from start but the relevant neighborhood is around endPos. The k=100 cap further silently truncates candidates in dense scenes, so genuine high-speed collisions (the exact case CCD exists for) can be missed with no diagnostic.

Fix: Seed the broad phase from the swept AABB (union of start and end positions inflated by shape radius), or query around the segment midpoint with radius >= sweepLength/2 + shapeRadius + buffer, and/or use a range query rather than a fixed k=100 kNN. At minimum document and surface the truncation when nearbyEntities.size()==100.

title: [lucien] DistanceConstraint warm-start uses lambda*deltaTime but solver accumulates raw impulse (unit mismatch)
description:
lucien/src/main/java/com/hellblazer/luciferase/lucien/collision/physics/constraints/DistanceConstraint.java:112, 141-145
Severity: Medium | Category: bug

solve() accumulates an impulse: `lambda += deltaLambda` where deltaLambda = effectiveMass*(-velAlongAxis + bias), i.e. lambda is in impulse units. But prepare() warm-starts with `applyImpulse(axis, lambda * deltaTime)` — multiplying the stored impulse by deltaTime, which is dimensionally wrong (impulse*time). The warm-start therefore re-applies a scaled-down fraction of last frame's impulse, so warm starting is ineffective (or scaled by an arbitrary dt), defeating its convergence purpose and producing dt-dependent joint stiffness.

Fix: Warm-start with the stored impulse directly: `applyImpulse(axis, lambda);` (drop the *deltaTime), matching the accumulation convention in solve(). Confirm ContactConstraint, which warm-starts with the raw normalImpulseSum, as the correct precedent.

The *deltaTime makes warm-start impulse off by the timestep factor. | acceptance: line 112 reads applyImpulse(axis, lambda); existing DistanceConstraintOrientationTest still green; add a regression test that runs prepare()->solve() over multiple substeps and asserts warm-started converged lambda is timestep-independent | blast-radius: applyImpulse/prepare are private/internal to DistanceConstraint; no external callers of the warm-start path; only Constraint.prepare() contract (called by physics solver loop) affected

title: [lucien-distributed] BatchQueue creates a per-rank ScheduledExecutorService that defeats the documented batching and leaks the wall-clock-scheduled task
description:
lucien-distributed/src/main/java/com/hellblazer/luciferase/lucien/balancing/grpc/BalanceCoordinatorClient.java:594-639
Severity: Medium | Category: resource-leak

Each BatchQueue (one per targetRank, created lazily in requestRefinementBatched line 255) allocates its own newSingleThreadScheduledExecutor (line 591). The flush() at line 622 then iterates the batch and sends each request individually via stub.requestRefinement in a loop (lines 623-637) - so 'batching' provides zero wire-level batching (admitted in the line-621 comment) while paying the cost of N scheduled-executor threads. More importantly, the timeout scheduling uses timeoutMillis with no Clock injection and the scheduler is only shut down on client.shutdown(); a BatchQueue whose target is never flushed-to-full retains a live single-thread executor. For many ranks this is N leaked threads.

title: [lucien-distributed] ProtobufConverters stamps ghost timestamps with System.currentTimeMillis() and reads it twice non-atomically
description:
lucien-distributed/src/main/java/com/hellblazer/luciferase/lucien/forest/ghost/grpc/ProtobufConverters.java:204-207, 259-262
Severity: Medium | Category: clock-injection

ghostElementToProtobuf (204-207) and ghostLayerToProtobufBatch (259-262) build a protobuf Timestamp by calling System.currentTimeMillis() TWICE - once for seconds, once for nanos. Besides the clock-injection violation, the two reads are not atomic: if the millisecond rolls over between the two calls, seconds and the sub-second nanos component disagree (seconds from before the tick, nanos from after), producing a timestamp off by up to ~1s. A utility class cannot hold injected state easily, so the Clock/now-millis must be threaded in by callers.

Fix: Capture long now = clock.currentTimeMillis() once and derive both seconds and nanos from that single value; pass a Clock (or a precomputed timestamp) into the converter from the caller rather than reading System time inside the converter.

title: [misc] Injected Clock is dead code — staleness/expiry use caller-supplied time, so setClock() does nothing
description:
/Users/hal.hildebrand/git/Luciferase/simulation/src/main/java/com/hellblazer/luciferase/simulation/ghost/GhostLifecycleStateMachine.java:170, 291-305, 319-333, 412-414
Severity: Medium | Category: hollow-stub / false-determinism

The class advertises 'Clock injection for deterministic testing' (javadoc line 38) and exposes setClock() (412), which GhostStateManager.setClock() dutifully propagates (GhostStateManager.java:204). But the clock field (170) is NEVER read anywhere in the class. isStale()/isExpired()/findExpired() all compute staleness from the caller-passed `currentTime` argument (297, 325). The injected clock is a no-op. This is a false determinism signal: a test that injects a TestClock here and then drives time through it will silently exercise nothing — the determinism actually comes entirely from whoever passes currentTime. Any future maintainer relying on setClock() to control this component's notion of 'now' will get wrong behavior.

Fix: Either (a) delete the clock field + setClock() and the GhostStateManager propagation, documenting that time is always caller-supplied; or (b) add no-arg overloads isStale(id)/isExpired(id)/expireStaleGhosts() that read clock.currentTimeMillis() and make the existing currentTime-arg methods delegate, so the injected clock is genuinely the time source.

Verify evidence: Confirmed by reading the full file. The `clock` field is declared at line 170 (`private volatile Clock clock = Clock.system();`) and assigned only in `setClock()` (lines 412-414: `this.clock = Objects.requireNonNull(clock, ...)`). It is never read by any method. All time-based logic uses the caller-supplied argument, not the field: `isStale()` computes `long timeSinceUpdate = currentTime - state.lastUpdateAt;` (line 297), `isExpired()` does the same (line 325), `findExpired(long currentTime)` delegates to `isExpired(entityId, currentTime)` (line 346), and `expireStaleGhosts`/`expireStaleGhostsReturningIds` thread `currentTime` through (lines 360-361, 377). `onCreate`/`onUpdate` use the caller-passed `timestamp`. Meanwhile the class javadoc advertises "Clock injection for deterministic testing" (line 37) and the usage example shows `lifecycle.setClock(testClock); // Optional: for deterministic testing` (line 60). So setClock() is genuinely a no-op on this component's notion of 'now' — dead code plus a misleading determinism signal, exactly as claimed. Severity lowered from High to Medium: there is no runtime correctness failure or data loss — the component is in fact deterministic b

title: [simulation] getQuorumResult cannot distinguish failed/timed-out proposals from still-pending ones
description:
simulation/src/main/java/com/hellblazer/luciferase/simulation/consensus/committee/CommitteeServiceImpl.java:74-82, 123-143
Severity: Medium | Category: correctness/observability

submitMigrationProposal only populates proposalResults in the whenComplete success branch (ex==null, lines 74-78). When the consensus future completes EXCEPTIONALLY (TimeoutException from CommitteeVotingProtocol.handleTimeout, or IllegalStateException from rollbackOnViewChange), the ex!=null branch (lines 79-81) merely logs a warn and never records any result. Consequently getQuorumResult (line 124) finds resultRef==null and returns the generic error 'Proposal result not yet available' (line 142) FOREVER for that proposalId — identical to the response for a proposal that is genuinely still voting. A proposer polling for the outcome of an aborted/timed-out migration can never learn it was rejected vs. still in flight, so it cannot safely retry or release the entity. This is the RDR-004-class failure shape (ACK/return path silently loses the failure outcome) applied to the quorum-result query path. Note a rejected-but-completed proposal (result==false) IS handled correctly because false is non-null.

Fix: In the whenComplete ex!=null branch, record a terminal failure outcome (e.g. store a tri-state Optional<Boolean>/enum {PENDING, APPROVED, REJECTED, FAILED} or a dedicated failure marker) keyed by proposalId, and have getQuorumResult surface FAILED distinctly from not-yet-available. Add a test that times out a proposal and asserts getQuorumResult returns a terminal failure, not the pending error.

Verify evidence: Confirmed by reading the cited code. In submitMigrationProposal (CommitteeServiceImpl.java:74-82), proposalResults is populated ONLY in the success branch (ex==null, lines 75-78). The exceptional branch (lines 79-81) merely logs `log.warn("Proposal {} consensus failed", ...)` and records nothing. title: [misc] A new JVM shutdown hook is registered on every initialize() call and never removed

title: [misc] Unbounded cached thread pool + no accepted-connection/session cap -> thread & FD exhaustion DoS

title: [simulation] Split conservation check reads accountant counts non-atomically (TOCTOU) under partial-move failure

Snapshot the relevant entity sets once under the lock rather than re-reading. title: [render] ESVTGPUMemory is not AutoCloseable and relies on deprecated finalize() to free native memory
description:
render/src/main/java/com/hellblazer/luciferase/esvt/gpu/ESVTGPUMemory.java:241-271
Severity: Medium | Category: RESOURCE LEAK

The class allocates native off-heap memory via memAlignedAlloc (line 84) and a GPU SSBO, but exposes only dispose() and is NOT AutoCloseable, so it cannot be used in try-with-resources and is easy to leak. Its only safety net is finalize() (lines 264-271), which is deprecated for removal, runs nondeterministically (or never), and on the finalizer thread calls dispose() -> memAlignedFree plus OpenGL nodeSSBO.close() — invoking GL from the finalizer thread without a current context is itself unsafe. Every caller that forgets dispose() leaks native + GPU memory until/if the finalizer runs.

Fix: Implement AutoCloseable with close() delegating to dispose(); make dispose() idempotent (already is). Remove the finalize() override (or replace with a java.lang.ref.Cleaner that frees ONLY the native ByteBuffer, never touches GL). Audit callers to use try-with-resources.

Verify evidence: Confirmed by reading the file. Line 41 `public final class ESVTGPUMemory` does NOT implement AutoCloseable; native memory is allocated at line 84 (`memAlignedAlloc`) and a GPU SSBO (`nodeSSBO`). The only release path is `dispose()` (lines 241-262: `nodeSSBO.close()` at 248, `memAlignedFree(nodeBuffer)` at 256) — there is no `close()`, so try-with-resources is impossible. The sole safety net is the `finalize()` override (lines 264-271), which on the !disposed path logs and calls `dispose()`, thereby invoking OpenGL (`nodeSSBO.close()`) from the finalizer thread without a current GL context — genuinely unsafe. finalize() is deprecated-for-removal and nondeterministic. All cited facts hold. Adjusted to Medium rather than High: the leak is conditional on a caller forgetting dispose(), a (flawed) safety net does free the native buffer, no concrete leaking caller is cited, and the SSBO is also managed by UnifiedResourceManager (line 55). The proper fix is implement AutoCloseable/close() and drop finalize() — a legitimate maintainability+safety defect, but not a guaranteed High-severity leak.

title: [lucien] findIntervalEnd() linearly scans the entire Morton range, defeating the BIGMIN optimization and risking O(range) blowups
description:
lucien/src/main/java/com/hellblazer/luciferase/lucien/sfc/LitmaxBigmin.java:184-201
Severity: Medium | Category: correctness

findIntervalEnd increments the Morton code by 1 (next = current + 1) and decodes/tests containment one cell at a time until a cell falls outside the box, walking up to maxMorton. The class doc and bigmin() comment (lines 228-233) claim O(interval-count) instead of O(morton-range), but the interval-END extension is still a per-code linear walk. For a large query box at a fine level the Morton range between minMorton and maxMorton can be in the billions, so a single deep interval extension can iterate astronomically (each step a decode), making cellsQ pathologically slow despite producing correct results. The advertised performance contract (Luciferase-lield) is only half-met.

Fix: Replace the linear +1 walk with a LITMAX-based interval-end computation (compute the largest contiguous in-box Morton run from intervalStart using the same bit-window refinement bigmin uses), so interval extension is O(bits) not O(cells). Add a benchmark/regression with a large box asserting bounded decode count.

Verify evidence: Confirmed by reading lines 184-201. `findIntervalEnd` does perform a per-Morton-code linear walk: `var next = current + 1; var coords = MortonCurve.decode(next);` then containment test, advancing one cell at a time until a cell falls outside the box, bounded only by `maxMorton`. The companion `bigmin()` comment (lines 228-233) explicitly claims the Tropf-Herzog rewrite achieves "O(interval-count) instead of O(morton-range)", yet the interval-END extension was not converted and remains a per-cell scan. So the advertised performance contract (Luciferase-lield) is indeed only half-met — interval-start finding skips out-of-box gaps via bit manipulation, but interval-end extension iterates every in-box cell. The defect is real.

Severity adjusted High -> Medium. The walk is NOT over the full min-to-max Morton range as the title implies ("walking up to maxMorton" / "iterate astronomically"). It is bounded by the number of IN-BOX contiguous cells, since the loop breaks the moment a code leaves the box (line 196-197). Total work summed across all `findIntervalEnd` calls equals the count of cells inside the query box — i.e. bounded by the query result cardinality you would have to enumerate

title: [misc] Inverse transformation sets final fields via reflection, defeating final semantics and JPMS encapsulation
description:
/Users/hal.hildebrand/git/Luciferase/dyada-java/src/main/java/com/dyada/transformations/LinearTransformation.java:383-406
Severity: Medium | Category: DESIGN / correctness-fragility

createInverseTransformation() constructs the inverse then mutates the `final` fields cachedDeterminant and cachedInverse on the new instance through reflection (setAccessible + Field.set). Writing to final fields after construction is not guaranteed visible to other threads under the JMM (final-field freeze already happened at constructor exit), so a LinearTransformation handed to another thread may observe null cachedInverse/cachedDeterminant and recompute or NPE. It is also brittle under the module-info.java JPMS boundary (setAccessible on a final field can throw InaccessibleObjectException depending on open-ness) and silently couples correctness to reflection succeeding. The catch wraps any failure in a RuntimeException at call time rather than construction time.

Fix: Add a private constructor that accepts the precomputed determinant and inverse and assigns them to the final fields directly (the normal way to build a back-linked inverse). Remove all reflection. This restores final-field publication guarantees and removes the JPMS hazard.

Verify evidence: Confirmed by reading LinearTransformation.java. cachedDeterminant (line 24) and cachedInverse (line 25) are declared `private final`. createInverseTransformation (lines 383-406) constructs `new LinearTransformation(inverseMatrix, false)`, whose constructor sets both final fields to null (lines 73-74), then mutates them post-construction via reflection: getDeclaredField + setAccessible(true) + Field.set (lines 393-399), wrapping any failure in a RuntimeException at call time (lines 401-403). Every technical assertion holds: (1) the final-field freeze completes at constructor exit (line 76) with both fields=null, so the reflective writes at 395/399 occur after the freeze with no JMM happens-before guarantee to threads that obtain the reference — a stale null is a legal observation; (2) NPE exposure is real and unguarded at inverse() line 139 (`cachedInverse.transform(...)`), though determinant() reads are null-guarded (lines 158, 252) so they degrade to recompute rather than NPE; (3) reflective write to a final field is fundamentally unsound and is the canonical InaccessibleObjectException risk under a JPMS module boundary. Adjusted High->Medium: the hazard is genuine and the design

title: [misc] Owns ForkJoinPool + non-daemon fixedThreadPool but is not AutoCloseable; owner AbstractSpatialIndex also not AutoCloseable
description:
/Users/hal.hildebrand/git/Luciferase/lucien/src/main/java/com/hellblazer/luciferase/lucien/ParallelBulkOperations.java:52-53, 70-74, 229-237
Severity: Medium | Category: resource-leak

ParallelBulkOperations creates a ForkJoinPool or Executors.newFixedThreadPool(config.getThreadCount()) (lines 70-74). newFixedThreadPool uses non-daemon threads, so if shutdown() (line 229) is never called these threads keep the JVM alive and leak. shutdown() exists but the class does not implement AutoCloseable, and AbstractSpatialIndex holds it as a volatile field (parallelOperations) exposing only shutdownParallelOperations() (1271) while AbstractSpatialIndex itself is not AutoCloseable. Nothing structurally forces cleanup; any index that lazily inits parallel ops and is GC'd without an explicit shutdown leaks two thread pools. configureParallelOperations swapping the volatile (per class doc) can also orphan a prior pool with no shutdown.

Fix: Implement AutoCloseable on ParallelBulkOperations (close()->shutdown()+awaitTermination) and on AbstractSpatialIndex (close() shuts down parallel ops + ghosts). Use a daemon ThreadFactory for the fixed pool. On volatile swap in configureParallelOperations, shutdown the replaced instance.

Verify evidence: Confirmed by reading the source. ParallelBulkOperations holds `ForkJoinPool workStealingPool` and `ExecutorService fixedThreadPool` (lines 52-53). The constructor (lines 70-74) creates `new ForkJoinPool(config.getThreadCount())` when work-stealing is on, else `Executors.newFixedThreadPool(config.getThreadCount())` — the latter uses the default ThreadFactory whose threads are non-daemon. `shutdown()` exists (lines 229-237) but the class (line 43) does NOT implement AutoCloseable/Closeable. The owner AbstractSpatialIndex (lines 86-88) implements only SpatialIndex and ShapeWeightProvider — not AutoCloseable — holds `volatile parallelOperations` (line 125) and exposes only shutdownParallelOperations() (line 1271). configureParallelOperations (lines 358-362) reassigns the volatile to a new instance without shutting down the prior one, orphaning a live pool. All factual claims are accurate. Severity adjusted from High to Medium: (1) the non-daemon-thread JVM-pinning concern applies ONLY to the non-default useWorkStealing=false path — ForkJoinPool threads are daemon by default, so the work-stealing path does not pin the JVM; (2) newFixedThreadPool creates threads lazily on task submission

title: [misc] updateBatchParallel silently reassigns NEW entity IDs on 'update', invalidating caller-held IDs
description:
/Users/hal.hildebrand/git/Luciferase/lucien/src/main/java/com/hellblazer/luciferase/lucien/ParallelBulkOperations.java:239-247
Severity: Medium | Category: design/data-identity

updateBatchParallel (named an update) reinserts each entity via insert(), which assigns a brand-new EntityID; the input ids become stale and the returned list holds different ids (documented at lines 245-246 as 'pre-existing'). An update operation that silently changes entity identity is a correctness trap: any external map/index/reference keyed on the original IDs now dangles, and the operation's name promises mutation-in-place. Being long-standing and documented does not make it safe — it is a silent data-identity loss for callers who don't read the javadoc.

Fix: Provide a true in-place update that preserves EntityID (remove+reinsert under the same id), or rename to make the id-reassignment semantics impossible to miss (e.g. reinsertBatchWithNewIds) and have it return an old->new id mapping rather than only the new ids.

Verify evidence: Confirmed by reading ParallelBulkOperations.java:248-283. updateBatchParallel performs remove+reinsert: line 268 `spatialIndex.removeEntity(id)` then line 269 `ID newId = spatialIndex.insert(newPos, level, content)`, and line 271 adds `newId` (not the original `id`) to the returned `updatedIds`. insert() assigns a brand-new EntityID, so the input ids become stale and the returned list holds different ids — an external map/index keyed on original IDs would dangle. This matches the description and is corroborated by the javadoc at lines 245-246: "each update reinserts via insert, which assigns a NEW entity id; the returned list holds the new ids and the input ids become stale after this call." The defect is real (data-identity loss on an operation named "update"). However, severity is reduced from High to Medium: the behavior is explicitly documented in the method's javadoc as a known "(pre-existing)" ID-semantics contract, the disclosure mitigates the silent-trap risk for callers who read the API, and it is intentional pre-existing design rather than a latent code bug. It remains a genuine API design wart (an "update" that changes entity identity) worth fixing or renaming, hence not

title: [common] removeRange() does not validate fromIndex/toIndex bounds — silent corruption or ArrayIndexOutOfBounds
description:
common/src/main/java/com/hellblazer/luciferase/common/FloatArrayList.java:181-188
Severity: Medium | Category: Edge case / memory safety

removeRange only checks `toIndex < fromIndex`. It never validates `fromIndex >= 0`, `toIndex <= size`, or `fromIndex <= size`. A call with toIndex > size makes `System.arraycopy(array, toIndex, array, fromIndex, size - toIndex)` use a NEGATIVE length (size - toIndex < 0) — IndexOutOfBoundsException at best, and with fromIndex negative arraycopy can corrupt or read out of bounds. `size -= (toIndex - fromIndex)` can also drive size negative, leaving the list in a corrupt state that later get()/remove() trust. java.util.ArrayList validates both ends and throws a precise IOOBE.

Fix: Add: `if (fromIndex < 0 || toIndex > size) throw new IndexOutOfBoundsException(...)` before the arraycopy, matching ArrayList.removeRange semantics. Apply the identical fix in IntArrayList.removeRange (line 226) and ShortArrayList.

Verify evidence: Confirmed by reading FloatArrayList.java lines 181-188. removeRange() validates ONLY `if (toIndex < fromIndex) throw IndexOutOfBoundsException`. It never checks `fromIndex >= 0`, `toIndex <= size`, or `fromIndex <= size`. Line 186 `System.arraycopy(array, toIndex, array, fromIndex, size - toIndex)` produces a negative length when `toIndex > size` (arraycopy throws IOOBE), and a negative/invalid destIndex when `fromIndex < 0`. Line 187 `size -= (toIndex - fromIndex)` can leave size in a corrupt (e.g. wrong/negative) state for input combinations that don't trigger an immediate arraycopy throw, after which get()/remove() trust the bad size. This contrasts with sibling methods in the same file (addFloat line 206, ensureIndexInRange line 228-229) which DO bounds-check both ends, and with java.util.ArrayList which throws precise IOOBE. The defect is genuine and is a memory-safety / edge-case validation gap. Adjusted from High to Medium: it is a defensive-validation omission requiring caller misuse to trigger (no live caller passing bad bounds was demonstrated), and the most common bad-input case fails loudly via arraycopy rather than silently corrupting; the silent-corruption path is rea

title: [misc] Cache size bound and LRU eviction are racy and non-atomic across two ConcurrentHashMaps
description:
/Users/hal.hildebrand/git/Luciferase/dyada-java/src/main/java/com/dyada/performance/DyAdaCache.java:73-84, 112-130
Severity: Medium | Category: CONCURRENCY

DyAdaCache claims thread-safe LRU+TTL but coordinates two independent maps (cache, accessTimes) with no locking. put() (line 77-83) puts into cache, then accessTimes, then checks size()>maxSize and evicts; under concurrent puts the size check and evictLRU() race, so the cache can exceed maxSize and multiple threads can each evict, over-evicting live entries. evictLRU() (line 112-129) does an unsynchronized full scan of accessTimes selecting a min, then removes from both maps — between scan and removal another thread can re-touch that key, so the most-recently-used entry can be evicted (LRU violated). accessTimes can also leak entries for keys whose CacheEntry was evicted by a different path. Statistics aside, this is a correctness bug for the eviction invariant the class advertises.

Fix: Either back the cache with a single structure (e.g. Caffeine, or a synchronized LinkedHashMap in accessOrder mode), or guard put/evict/get-touch with a single lock. At minimum keep one source of truth (store access time inside CacheEntry) so eviction and membership cannot diverge across two maps.

Verify evidence: Confirmed by reading the cited lines. put() (lines 73-84) does cache.put → accessTimes.put → `if (cache.size() > maxSize) evictLRU()` with no locking; evictLRU() (lines 112-130) does an unsynchronized full scan of accessTimes for the min accessTime then cache.remove/accessTimes.remove on the captured lruKey. Claims verified: (1) Over-eviction — multiple concurrent puts can each pass the size check and each run evictLRU, removing more than one entry when only one was over-bound; size can also transiently exceed maxSize. (2) LRU violation — between the scan and `cache.remove(lruKey)`, another thread's get()/put() can accessTimes.put() (touch) the chosen key (lines 47/65/78), yet the stale lruKey is removed anyway, so a just-touched entry can be evicted. (3) Two-map non-atomicity (cache vs accessTimes) permits transient/orphan inconsistencies. The class JavaDoc explicitly advertises 'LRU eviction... and concurrent access' (lines 9-12), so the racy eviction breaks the advertised invariant — this is a genuine defect, not a false positive. Severity adjusted from High to Medium: this is a derived/recomputable performance cache (Morton/multiscale lookups, lines 184-304); the underlying Con
notes: ENRICHED 2026-06-04 | still-valid: yes | anchors: DyAdaCache.java two unsynchronized maps cache+accessTimes L15-16; put() L73-82 (put cache, put accessTimes L78, then size()>maxSize check L81 -> evictLRU L82) non-atomic; evictLRU L112-128 scans accessTimes picking min; CacheEntry record L162 (createdAt only, no access time) | test: mvn test -pl dyada-java -Dtest=DyAdaCacheTest | approach: Make one source of truth. Option A: replace both maps with a single synchronized LinkedHashMap(accessOrder=true) overriding removeEldestEntry for bounded LRU. Option B: guard put/get-touch/evict with one lock. Option C: store access time inside CacheEntry (extend the record) and drop the accessTimes map. Pick A or C to eliminate the cross-map race where size check and eviction interleave under concurrent puts. | acceptance: (1) single coherent structure or single lock; (2) concurrent-put stress test never exceeds maxSize and never NPEs from desynced maps; (3) LRU eviction order correct under contention; (4) DyAdaCacheTest green | blast-radius: dyada-java performance cache; check callers via grep DyAdaCache in dyada-java before changing public API (create/createLRU/put/get signatures should stay stable)

title: [lucien] findEntitiesIncludingGhosts / findNeighborsIncludingGhosts silently return zero ghosts
description:

Because the layer is never populated (createGhostElement is a no-op stub, and addGhostElement has no callers), the ghost branch of both queries always contributes nothing. That detector-owned layer is populated only via the boundary scan's createGhostElement hook, which in GhostBoundaryDetector.java:451-454 is a placeholder that only logs: `// Placeholder ghost creation - actual data would come via gRPC` / `log.trace(...)` — it never calls ghostLayer.addGhostElement.
